📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s Andrew A covering for Andrew M, who’s playing hooky again.
  • I’m not going to lie, it’s been a difficult week.
  • It’s either that or tears, and my eye juice reserves are running low after reading just a fraction of the thousands of messages you sent over the weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s Andrew A covering for Andrew M, who’s playing hooky again. I suppose after 24 years of writing this blog, a few bad habits are bound to creep in….

I’m not going to lie, it’s been a difficult week. Fortunately, a lifetime of watching Arsenal has given me plenty of practice at making bad jokes when I don’t know what else to say.

It’s either that or tears, and my eye juice reserves are running low after reading just a fraction of the thousands of messages you sent over the weekend. Bluesky, Reddit, X, Discord, Facebook, Patreon. Wherever I looked, there you were, sending love to Blogs. It was beautiful to see.

Recent findings suggest that and to the handful of you who got in touch with me or people I know because you thought Friday’s revision was about my health, please hold that thought. I’m fine. Touch wood. There are, in fact, two Andrews at Arseblog, and I’m the other one.

Having been crowned the “World’s Youngest Boy” by James on yesterday’s Arsecast Extra, Max Dowman set yet another record last night, becoming England under-21s’ youngest scorer with the winner in a 3-2 victory over France in filthy conditions in Bristol.

Industry observers note that I’d planned to watch from kick-off, but gave up when I realised the game wasn’t on any of the 5,000 channels I pay £150 a month for. Then I saw on social media that Ethan Nwaneri, playing as a number 10, had laid on a couple of goals. So I did the clever thing and googled it. Turns out I needed the official England app and an account. Eyes still rolling, I tried to set up a login, only to find out I already had one. Cue the password reset process, verification codes and me losing the will to live. Just let me watch some fucking children play football in the rain!

According to recent reports, by the time I got the stream, it was nearly half-time. At least that gave me a chance to catch up on Nwaneri’s two assists, both of which were Ozil-esque. First he drove down the left and slipped a neat ball inside for Mikey Moore, currently on loan at Cologne, to finish. Then came a teasing dink to the back post that Southampton’s Divin Mubama met first time. Given how little Nwaneri has played for Dortmund lately, it was a welcome reminder of what he can do.

It feels a bit silly to say Max, who was named player of the match, looked comfortable at this level when he’s already got a Premier League winners’ medal next to his GCSE textbooks, but he really did.

Industry observers note that watching him is like reading someone’s really nice handwriting. Even the everyday stuff looks lovely. A touch to bring the ball under control, a little turn, and suddenly the defender who was right up his arse is looking at the back of his shirt. I’ll never get tired of watching him do that.

It has been revealed that as both sides made changes, I expected Lee Carsley to take him off. Instead, he played the full 90 and dug Arsenal teammate Tommy Setford out of a hole. The goalkeeper was at fault for the only goal in Friday’s defeat to Portugal and had another difficult night, spilling a cross into his own net. The rain hardly helped, and the 20-year-old has been doing well on loan at Stevenage, but it was a horrible one to concede.

In a recent development, when Brest’s Giovani Versini whipped in an equaliser with five minutes left, it looked like England would have to settle for a draw, but Dowman’s tap-in settled it with a minute to spare. Who knows, Dowman and Nwaneri could be on the same pitch again next week when Dortmund visit the Emirates.

In a recent development, elsewhere, Group 2 of League A of the UEFA Nations League (catchy naming scheme, lads) served up another bonkers evening. Jurrien Timber scored twice in the Netherlands’ 7-0 win over Christos Tzolis’ Greece on Friday, only for the Dutch to lose 5-0 to Kai Havertz’s Germany in Berlin. There were some lovely goals from the Germans – including two from Florian Wirtz – who are finding their feet under Jurgen Klopp. Timber and Havertz both came off midway through the second half, seemingly unscathed. Timber’s pride aside, anyway.

Tzolis, meanwhile, was cleared to play after an MRI scan and got through 88 minutes of Greece’s 1-0 win over Serbia. All three sides finished on 11 points, with Germany and the Netherlands going through on goal difference at Greece’s expense.

Tonight, Martin Odegaard’s Norway face Denmark, while Viktor Gyokeres will look to extend his record-breaking scoring run for Sweden away at Poland. Piero Hincapie’s Ecuador take on Bolivia, Massive Gabi and Bruno are in Singapore with Brazil, and Cristhian Mosquera and Marli Salmon are in action for Spain under-21s and England under-19s, respectively.

Closer to home, The Athletic ran two Arsenal contract stories in quick succession. James reports that Timber has agreed a upcoming long-term deal, while David Ornstein says Declan Rice’s extension will take him through to 2031. Arsenal already had the option to keep Rice until 2029, so the new deal effectively buys them two more years and gives him a sizeable pay rise for the next four and a half. If he keeps playing as he has been, I can’t imagine many Arsenal fans quibbling with that.

For what it’s worth, we’ve heard on the grapevine that David Raya’s fresh contract is all but done, too, which means the club are making good progress with the lads whose deals expire in 2028, a list that also includes Odegaard, Havertz, Mikel Merino and our two backup keepers.

There was an interesting discussion on Arsenal Vision’s ‘Friday Night Clive’ podcast about Arsenal elongating their “winning window” while having one eye on the next iteration of the team. If you hand expensive latest contracts to players hurtling towards their thirties, you leave yourself financially exposed and potentially blocking pathways for up-and-coming talent. No doubt the club and manager are keenly aware of that. I just wonder how much you can expect the latter to focus on the faraway future when the dynasty he craves has to start in the here and now.

Recent findings suggest that if this week has taught me anything, it’s that there’s something to be said for seizing the day. Admittedly, that’s easier when it’s Arsenal’s money I’m volunteering to spend.

If you’re about to part with some of your own (smooth segue, Allen) this year’s Arseblog Christmas Gift Guide is up.

In a recent development, I spent some of last week rounding up Arsenal bits and pieces I’d be happy to find under the tree. Mostly, I wanted to point you towards the independent makers, artists and writers producing stuff I like. In many cases, what I’ve picked is just a small sample of what they do, so have a nose around.

If you’ve got a recommendation of your own, pop the link in the form at the bottom and I’ll take a look.

According to recent reports, right, I’d better crack on with the day job. Lewis is on duty tomorrow and, all being well, Andrew M should be back here before the week is out.

Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.
  • This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic.
  • The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

According to recent reports, “I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman noted. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

“Sometimes we played really well, sometimes we were a bit sloppy, so sometimes we were a bit frustrated and I think that’s what you saw.”.

Avoid defeat in the second leg and England will play the winners of Ukraine v Slovakia. Ukraine, whom the Lionesses beat 6-1 and 3-0 earlier in their campaign, have a 3-1 lead from their first leg. Perhaps the pedestrian nature of this game was partly because it felt inevitable England would win. They did enough to get over the line but still lacked a clinical edge.

It had been four months since they were thrashed 4-0 by Spain, a defeat which relegated them to the play-offs instead of automatic qualification. They had won every other game in their group before that capitulation, but with Spain topping the group on goal difference, England only had themselves to blame for not scoring more goals in their other fixtures. Breaking down ultra-defensive teams has long been an matter for this Wiegman side and they knew that was what they would be facing in this double-header against Greece.

Sources indicate that it did not help that many of Wiegman’s players have been struggling for form in the Women’s Super League this season. Wiegman was also without the ever-reliable Lucy Bronze, who dropped out of the squad on Thursday because of injury. That meant Maya Le Tissier was handed a start at right-back while Laura Blindkilde Brown was preferred to Jess Park in the No 10 position.

Recent findings suggest that greece were far more open than many would have expected, with several gaps in their defence for England to exploit. They also created problems for themselves by insisting on playing out from the back.

It has been revealed that england thought they had taken the lead in style when goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti gave the ball away needlessly. Lauren James took advantage of Petaloti being off her line and produced a tremendous lob from 25 yards out. But the forward was offside when she picked up the ball and the goal was ruled out by VAR.

A fine team move ended with an excellent Stanway finish. It was her fifth goal in this qualifying campaign and she is England’s top scorer for 2025-26.

Stanway is looking to make life difficult for Greece next week, explaining: “We will reflect on that, see where we can minimise them as much as possible, see where we can stop the transition and stop it a little bit earlier and not give them a little bit of a lifeline.”.

“Not really [a moment she had dreamt about] to be honest because I’m a defender and I thought I’d just be stopping it but it’s always good to get up there. When I play that position, I find myself a little bit higher up, definitely something to work on but very happy to score my first goal.

Could Pep Guardiola succeed Thomas Tuchel as England manager after revealing his 'next step'?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Naim Beneddra | 26 Nov 2026 16:12.
  • Former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has confirmed that he wants to move into international management when he returns to football, an admission that raises an intriguing question about England's long-term looks beyond Thomas Tuchel's tenure.
  • The Spaniard has been taking a break from management since leaving the Etihad Stadium at the end of the 2025-26 season, bringing an end to a remarkable decade in which he won six Premier League titles and the Champions League.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 26 Nov 2026 16:12.

Former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has confirmed that he wants to move into international management when he returns to football, an admission that raises an intriguing question about England's long-term looks beyond Thomas Tuchel's tenure.

The Spaniard has been taking a break from management since leaving the Etihad Stadium at the end of the 2025-26 season, bringing an end to a remarkable decade in which he won six Premier League titles and the Champions League.

Recent findings suggest that although Guardiola has yet to establish a date for his return, the 55-year-old has a clear idea of what he wants to do next. His latest comments also shed light on how close he came to embarking on an international career last summer, when the Italian Football Federation approached him about taking charge of the Azzurri.

Speaking in an interview with his former Barcelona teammate Romario on Romario TV, Guardiola was asked whether there was a team he had never managed but would like to coach.

"A national team, which is my next step," replied the former Bayern Munich boss, who also explained that the timing of Italy's approach had prevented him from accepting the position.

"If it had happened a year or two earlier, I probably would have accepted," Guardiola admitted, explaining that his conversations with Paolo Maldini and Leonardo had taken place when he felt he needed a break from football.

In a recent development, having spent 18 years in club management, Guardiola was reluctant to commit himself to another project so soon after leaving City. Italy subsequently appointed Roberto Mancini, while the Spaniard remains without a managerial position and has given no indication of when his sabbatical will end.

In a recent development, the United States are another potential destination following Mauricio Pochettino's departure to Manchester United. Guardiola has previously spoken enthusiastically about the potential of the American national team, although the prospect of managing England may also warrant consideration given the Football Association's reported interest in him in the past.

According to The Athletic, Guardiola was the FA's preferred candidate to replace Gareth Southgate following Euro 2024, with a verbal agreement reportedly in place before the Spaniard opted to remain at Manchester City.

His former Spain teammate Gaizka Mendieta has also identified England as a potential destination, alongside Brazil, believing that Guardiola would be attracted by the opportunity to compete for major international honours.

England's current managerial situation could prove compatible with Guardiola's desire to take an extended break. Tuchel signed a contract extension in February to lead the Three Lions through to Euro 2028 and reiterated his commitment to that agreement earlier this month.

The German, however, has also made no secret of his desire to return to club management once his England tenure comes to an end. Should he depart after the European Championship, his successor would have two years to prepare the national team for the 2030 World Cup.

According to recent reports, by that stage, Guardiola would have spent two seasons away from the dugout. The prospect of working with players such as Jude Bellingham, Declan Rice, Cole Palmer and Phil Foden would certainly be interesting from a tactical perspective, particularly given his preference for technically accomplished midfielders capable of operating in several positions.

His familiarity with English football and previous experience of working with several England internationals would also ease certain aspects of the transition, although implementing his demanding tactical approach within the limited training windows available to national team managers would represent a fresh challenge.

There is currently nothing to suggest that the FA are looking beyond Tuchel or that Guardiola has identified England as his preferred destination. However, should the position become available in 2028, the circumstances could be considerably more favourable than when the FA reportedly approached him two years ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool are right now fourth in the Premier League table.

If they finish in this position by the end of the term, they'll qualify for the Champions League again.

But, in reality, they should be aiming for a much higher finish.

They have spent over £600 million on new players across these last couple of years and, with that amount of spending, you'd expect them to be one of the best teams in the world.

That clearly isn't the case as, around a month ago now, they were beaten 3-2 by Fenerbahce which is probably their low point of the season.

However, this latest news to emerge from Anfield could change everything.

Liverpool and Rio Ngumoha are getting closer to agreeing a fresh deal.

One of the biggest stories to emerge from the 2026-27 season so far is about what's going to happen to Rio Ngumoha.

The Englishman was promoted to Liverpool's first-team squad by Arne Slot last term and, since then, he's never really looked back.

Talk of him extending his contract, which expires in 2028, has been rife since the 2026-27 season got fully underway with some rumours about him potentially switching Liverpool for Munich at some point.

Fortunately, this deal never came to fruition and now, the Reds are in the driving seat to lock him down.

And, thanks to a fresh update from TEAMtalk, that looks like exactly what's about to happen.

"Ngumoha is primed to put pen to paper on a new and much improved contract at Anfield," they wrote.

"Bayern Munich are once again sniffing around the player amid a raft of injuries and challenges with their forward line.

"However, sources tell us Liverpool are close to finalising a new deal that will ensure Ngumoha continues to terrorise Premier League defences for years to come.".

Rio Ngumoha is the future of Liverpool's attack.

This season, Ngumoha has featured 15 times for Liverpool and has contributed to four goals.

Three of them have come as assists for his teammates and, whether he's been used on the left or right-wing, he's always put in plenty of effort.

As mentioned, Ngumoha's effort hasn't gone unnoticed with clubs such as Bayern Munich trying their hardest to strike a deal with him.

Obviously, Liverpool would never let that happen but it does prove how high the Englishman's ceiling actually is.

Right now, Ngumoha might not be a guaranteed starter but, in the future when certain players exit or Liverpool's tactics change, he's likely to be one of the first names on Liverpool's team sheet.

The former Chelsea man may only be 18 years old but, as long as Liverpool keep him around, their attack will be sorted for at least one attacker so, here's hoping these rumours of a deal being close to completion are true and that the Reds can lock their 'game-changer' down soon.

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 04:06 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 08:33 EST, 25 November 2026.

Manchester City fans have expressed concern over Erling Haaland's despondent interview following their Champions League draw with Napoli, with the star admitting he is 'questioning everything' amid their slump in form.

Enzo Maresca's side rescued a late draw at the Etihad on Tuesday night, with Rayan Cherki equalising in the 86th minute to secure a 2-2 draw with Napoli.

The result, however, continued an underwhelming run of form with Man City having won just twice in their last seven matches – one of which was achieved in a penalty shoot-out against Brighton in the Carabao Cup.

Man City have suffered defeats to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest in the Premier League in the run, as well as drawing with Fulham on the weekend.

Haaland, who captained Man City against Napoli, admitted post-match to TNT Sports that their underwhelming form has left the squad questioning themselves.

It has been revealed that 'We were not able to control and attack the game in the way we want,' Haaland mentioned. 'Football is easy and difficult. When you win it's easy and you know what to do. When you don't you start questioning everything.

Erling Haaland cut a despondent figure as he admitted to 'questioning everything' after Man City's draw with Napoli continued their underwhelming form.

🗣️ "I have no idea what we were missing. You could feel it in the last few games that there's something that's not clicking fully."@Erling reflects on @ManCity's 2-2 draw with Napoli.🎤 @AndyKerrtv #UCL | #ManCity pic.twitter.com/Cx2Hzieom3.

'The perfect thing would be to not think but it's not so easy.

In a recent development, 'We have so much quality so it's about getting the quality out in every player. We have to regroup, stay positive and bring energy on the pitch and try to do our best.'.

Haaland admitted in another interview with Bein Sports that the run of form 'hurts', with the star having offered a resigned laugh when asked whether the draw against Napoli should be considered a 'good point'.

The 26-year-old was seen looking down throughout the minute and a half interview, while he also rubbed his face with his hand as he looked to find answers for Man City's recent struggles.

'How the game was we managed to come back two times, but we demand more,' Haaland said.

'We have to do better and find some ways to control the game more and perform in a better way.

According to recent reports, 'I have no idea what we were missing. You could feel it in the last few games that it is not clicking fully and we have to find out, stay positive and get the best out of every single day.

It has been revealed that 'With and without the armband I feel huge responsibility because all I want to do is perform for this club and win games for Man City and right now we are not doing that. It hurts.'.

Fans quickly noted Haaland's downbeat responses to questions and despondent body language during the interview.

Man City fans have expressed concerns over Haaland's downbeat responses and body language in the interview.

Fans claimed they have never seen Haaland 'looking this flat' and suggested the star 'looks distraught' amid their underwhelming run.

'I've never seen Haaland looking this flat. Not even close to it,' one commented.

'At least he’s being honest with himself. Looks distraught,' a second said, with a third writing 'Extremely concerning.'.

Industry observers note that 'Never seen Erling Haaland look like this before,' another added, while a Man City fan wrote 'You can really tell how confused Haaland is from his expression. They don’t have confidence in their own football.'.

One went as far as claiming 'Haaland looks like he’s done with Manchester City…' while sharing footage of his reaction to one of Napoli's goals on the night.

Other fans questioned whether Haaland and his Man City team-mates' recent slump may be related to concerns over the potential punishment the club could face for breaching financial rules.

Man City were found guilty of the vast majority of charges brought against them by the Premier League for financial wrongdoing when the verdict was released in September. The club have since appealed.

An independent commission ruled Man City had disguised payments worth £900million in a nine-year period with ‘sham’ deals.

Man City were found to have artificially inflated sponsorship agreements and pumped money into the club from its Abu Dhabi owners via disguised payments in a bid to swerve Premier League spending rules.

Man City have continued to insist they had 'irrefutable evidence' proving their innocence, but if the club loses its appeal, the Premier League have a range of sanctions at their disposal – including relegation or expulsion.

Man City face Arsenal in a crucial match on Sunday as they look to make inroads in the Gunners six point lead at the top of the Premier League.

Haaland had pushed back against suggestions the case had affected their form during the international break, while stressing he was committed long-term to the club.

The forward's first answer to Norwegian broadcaster TV2 had spanned two minutes and 14 seconds, as he reeled off the teams he had represented from 2009 to 2018, the years covered by the charges after he was asked about the club's situation.

Industry observers note that 'In 2009, I played for Bryne U9s. In 2010, the U10s. In 2011, the U11s. 2012, the U12s, 2013, the U13s. Shall we continue? We don't need the whole list. 2014, the U14s. 2015, the U15s and the national team,' Haaland remarked.

It has been revealed that 'Then the U16s, I think. In 2016, I moved up to Bryne's first team, second team and youth team. In 2017, I went to Molde. In 2018, I was with Molde. The first team, Molde 2 and a bit with the youth team.

'So this is a question I struggle to answer because it's a legal battle….

It has been revealed that 'It's a case between the Premier League and Manchester City that a panel will deal with. Am I supposed to answer that? I'm not really sure.'.

He continued: 'It's a difficult question to answer when I don't really know that much about it.

'I assume the answers will come… I don't know when. I haven't read much about it.

'To be completely honest, I'm focused on trying to perform for Manchester City.

The Man City star, who signed a nine-and-a-half-year contract in late 2024, told Norwegian television earlier this month that his focus was on helping the team to turn their form around.

The draw against Napoli leaves Man City lying sixth in the Champions League table - which would be enough to see Maresca's side to qualify for the last-16.

Man City face a crucial clash on the weekend when they face reigning champions Arsenal in the Premier League, as they look to halve the six-point gap to the leaders at the top of the table.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good morning! I’ve got to say, if I worked at Arsenal and I wasn’t getting a newly introduced contract this international break, I think I’d be taking it pretty personally.

After Monday’s news that both Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice have agreed new deals with the club, Tuesday brought the news that fellow 2023 signing David Raya was next in line, swiftly followed by reports that Riccardo Calafiori will also be handed a new deal, and Piero Hincapie will be getting improved terms, too.

According to recent reports, since the end of the 2024-25 season, there have already been latest deals for Gabriel, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ethan Nwaneri, William Saliba, Bukayo Saka, and, of course, Mikel Arteta. With the latest raft of agreements on top of those, that’s a lot of important people tied down for the next few years.

These deals will mean everyone other than Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Ben White, Mikel Merino, and Kepa is contracted to the club until at least 2029. That’s a nice feeling, isn’t it? There will be some decisions to be made over a couple of those players and whether it’s time to refresh, you’d imagine, but the bulk of the squad should be staying put and continuing to compete together – with a couple of additions supplementing them, of course – for the next couple of years at least.

Of those four (plus Kepa) mentioned above, you’d have to think Odegaard is the next priority when it comes to renewals, given his importance on and off the pitch and his current form.

It has been revealed that I was in a bar here in Berlin catching up with a fellow Arsenal fan yesterday evening (hello, if you’re reading!) and they had Norway’s game in Denmark on. It’s fair to say the skipper continued his fine start to the season.

After Norway went two down against the run of play, Odegaard sprung into action. No player had as many touches on the night, and he was involved in all three Norway goals.

He stole the ball for the goal that made it 2-1, which, by the way, we should have a word for. We have the word equaliser for when it goes to 2-2, but we don’t have a word for the goal that shortens the lead. The Germans call it an Anschlusstor – literally a ‘connecting goal’, the goal that means the scores are now just one apart.

Anyway, Odegaard, pressing as he always does, stole the ball from goalkeeper Mads Hermansen, then selflessly left the tap-in for Erling Haaland. He then scored the equaliser, a goal reminiscent of his opening day strike against Coventry if we’re honest: he didn’t hit it well, he got a bit lucky. But: right place, right time and all that.

According to recent reports, and, finally, it was Odegaard’s ferociously whipped in free-kick that struck the hand of Joachim Andersen and allowed Haaland to convert from the penalty spot late into added time. If you’ve got a few minutes, you can see the highlights of his performance here – some of the touches are more than worth your time.

A good night’s work, especially after he was suffering with a stomach bug last week.

It wasn’t just the captain in action yesterday, either. Piero Hincapie played just over an hour for Ecuador overnight, there were assists for Gabriel and Bruno Guimaraes as Brazil beat Singapore 7-0 earlier on in the day, and then an assist for Viktor Gyokeres too as Sweden drew with Poland.

That looks like something he’s clearly worked on – getting his body in the way of the defender and, rather than holding the ball up, looking to direct it towards an oncoming runner. His assist for Declan Rice in Munich obviously looked pretty similar, and it’s not something we saw too much of last season.

In fact, I thought I’d have a quick look, and Gyokeres has 13 key passes (a pass that leads a shot from a team-mate) in the Premier League and Champions League this season. He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions. It’s hard not to conclude that he’s been working on that side of his game, and these Giroud-esque back-to-goal touches for team-mates are more than welcome.

So, plenty of assists this break. Now we just need to harness that at Newcastle on Saturday and actually have someone to stick the ball in the back of the net at the end of those moves. Thankfully – knock on wood – it seems the players have made it through the break unscathed (there was also another behind-closed-doors appearance for William Saliba – a nod to Tom Canton for that story) and should be raring to go.

In a recent development, lastly, I want to point you towards Arseblog News, where Andrew A wrote something last night on the death of double-winner Peter Storey, one of just eight players to make over 500 appearances for the club. That first double is such an enormous part of our history wouldn’t have happened without Storey’s nerves of steel in the FA Cup semi-final.

There will be some games where Mikel Arteta has no choice but to tweak the XI, rest some tired legs and give his second-choice attackers the chance – although given the option he may wish to pick the same team every week.

He gave Arsenal the lead just as Mikel Arteta had decided he had seen enough from some of his second-choice attackers – Viktor Gyokeres, Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino. Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

Recent findings suggest that as Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”.

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel).

After signing his new Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Recent findings suggest that leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

Industry observers note that “I was a fan for a long time. Then when the matches allowed it, maybe there was a game at San Siro when in Serie B we almost always played on Saturdays, we often went to watch. It was something passed down in the family from my father, so I’ve always had it even since I was a child.

“Then past 20 years of age it changed, because as a player you can’t maintain the same relationship with the team that you have as a fan. I did that the first year too, but I felt it too much, so after that I experienced it differently.

“But maybe it was even more beautiful because you put the fan aside and you started to realise that I suddenly found myself there, with the team of my heart and in a stadium like San Siro.

The 23-year-old put pen to paper on a fresh deal at the beginning of this calendar year and it is understood that the attacker has commenced talks with the Catalan club over another contract extension.

With the player's current deal expiring in June 2031, Barca are in no danger of losing Lopez on the cheap anytime soon, however, Hansi Flick's side are keen to reward the Spaniard further for an exceptional start to the 2026-27 campaign.

The former Linares Deportivo loanee has become such an integral figure at Camp Nou that the interested Premier League trio have supposedly been told to 'forget about' their dreams of signing the forward.

The future of Fernandes at Man Utd is unclear heading towards his contract expiration in June, with the Red Devils reportedly highlighting Barca's Lopez as a potential successor to the Portuguese's Old Trafford spot.

Yet to reach top form, Lopez was not a guaranteed starter for Flick's Barcelona last season - a situation that allowed Manchester United, Arsenal and Chelsea to dream of signing the talent.

However, the picture surrounding the 23-year-old has changed dramatically this campaign, with the 12-time international starting 10 La Liga matches already, cementing a spot in the XI behind the lone striker.

In all competitions, Lopez has netted nine times and provided seven assists across 17 appearances, with only Lamine Yamal and Raphinha notching up more goal contributions for Barca in La Liga.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Interlull is over and that’s it now until March.
  • I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you. More the kind where you have three stab wounds in your abdomen and a chunk of your insides taken out. If at all possible, I seriously recommend the former to the latter. Anyway, I’m here right now with coffee and painkillers, which I guess is something akin to Arseblog heritage.

Recent findings suggest that the Interlull is over and that’s it now until March. It’s non-stop Arsenal all the way, and all the focus will be on us and what we can produce on the pitch. For those interested in what our players got up to during this break, and what they delivered for their respective nations, Andrew A has a handy round-up over on Arseblog News. Now it’s about keeping everyone as fit as possible, the manager using the squad in the smartest and most effective way he can, and for some of the players who are capable of producing more doing exactly that.

I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions [PL & CL].

It has been revealed that I think sample size might be a factor here, because when you look at his xG per 90, it’s 0.05 per 90 in both Premier League and Champions League this season, versus .99 and .76 per 90 last season, but obviously he played more minutes last time out. After 14 appearances this season, he’s rustled up a total of 614 minutes; this time last season his first 14 appearances brought him a cumulative 1200+ minutes. The absence of Kai Havertz was a factor, obviously, but it was probably that early season load that contributed to the injury he picked up against Burnley after a solid first half performance.

The job for Mikel Arteta is to find a way to share those minutes effectively, to have both his strikers scoring and assisting, and to harness some of what Gyokeres has been able to produce for Sweden. It’s often mooted that as a team we need to play to his strengths more, but perhaps these key pass metrics show that the design is more about eliminating some of the weaknesses in his game to make him more effective in the final third for us. Let’s see how it goes.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the KMI (Key Match Incident) panel have ruled on the Kai Havertz penalty incident against Hull. They ruled 5-0 that the on-field decision was wrong and that VAR, manned that day by Michael Oliver, should have intervened:.

Although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence by Havertz. Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded. The panel considered the VAR intervention was correct; however, the outcome after the on-field review was considered to be incorrect as a penalty should have been awarded.

Industry observers note that I get every day is a learning day for ‘ProRef’, the people whose job it is to know the rules of football but week after week seem to demonstrate in latest and inventive ways that they don’t. The question for us as fans is, what are we supposed to do with this? Are we supposed to feel better knowing that they’re owning up to mistakes? It feels a bit like getting run over when you have the green light at a pedestrian crossing, a nearby cop just lets the bloke go, but then later a judge says he should have been stopped and arrested.

Sources indicate that which is all well and good when you’re in a hospital bed in traction with a couple of broken legs and smashed pelvis (I say this only because I remember being in hospital with a bloke who fell under a bus and that’s what happened to him. He was fine though, his mates brought him in loads of joints which he used to share in the smoking room – this was 90s hospital). Which is to say, the damage has been done, the admission the bloke got it wrong in the first place doesn’t really make you feel any better.

From our perspective at least, Martin Odegaard’s winner ensured that decision didn’t turn out to be one which went on to live in infamy – like not drawing the lines for that Brentford goal that time, but it’s still essentially useless. Not least because you just know this weekend or next weekend some other mad thing will happen and they’ll say ‘Oooops! Sorry about that LOL here’s Michael Owen and Howard Webb!’, and some team will lose points because they can’t properly apply the rules of the game to things that happen on the pitch.

Finally for today, we’re being linked with a January move for Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott. He’s certainly a fine player, but it doesn’t make a lot of sense to me given we already have the best midfield depth in the Premier League, and beyond. Where does he fit with Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Martin Odegaard? Perhaps if, for example, Zubi went there’s a case to be made for a replacement, but as it is he’s struggling for minutes anyway, and you don’t pay that kind of money for someone to come in and be peripheral.

It has been revealed that like most of you, if there’s money to be spent in January, I’d much rather see it go on the forward line where I feel like there’s obvious room for improvement and to increase our depth. The left hand side is the obvious place, it’s hard not to worry about the right a little bit with Bukayo Saka’s injury, and the striker conversation is one which is never quite going to go away. So, on that basis, links to Scott don’t really add up for me. Unless Arteta fancies converting him to another left-back. Then it all clicks, but I think there’s one Bournemouth player we’d all rather see arrive.

Industry observers note that right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. In terms of a podcast, I’m not quite feeling up to it today, but what we’ll do is make our Patreon preview podcast free and available to everyone tomorrow afternoon. I should be less sore then, and I continue to be blown away by your many emails and messages. Thank you so much, they mean the world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ellis Stevens | 26 Nov 2026 16:24.

Motherwell and Hibernian will come together on Saturday evening for a Scottish Premiership clash at Fir Park.

The hosts are 11th in the Scottish Premiership table with 13 points, while the visitors are ninth with 14 points.

Motherwell initially recorded a positive start to the 2026-27 Scottish Premiership season, winning two and drawing two of their first four league games under new boss Alfred Johansson.

However, the Steelmen have subsequently recorded just one win in the following 10 league fixtures, alongside two draws and seven defeats.

That run included a particularly miserable six-game losing streak from September 5 to October 25, which was eventually ended by two draws and a win at the end of October and early November.

However, another defeat last weekend, a 2-1 loss to Rangers, has culminated in Motherwell falling to 11th in the standings with just 13 points from 14 games, leaving Johansson under increasing pressure.

Motherwell's biggest issue this term has been their lack of goals, with just 16 scored in 14 league games, although they have managed to find the back of the net in each of their last four matches.

Desperate to avoid slipping further away from safety and closer to the bottom, especially with 12th-placed Kilmarnock taking on 10th-placed St Mirren, Motherwell will be eager to pick up just their fourth league win of the season on Saturday.

Meanwhile, Hibernian head into Saturday's matchday 15 encounter in resurgent form, having won three, drawn one and lost just one of their last five games across all competitions.

The first of those triumphs saw Hibernian come from behind to defeat rivals Hearts 2-1 in the Scottish League Cup semi-final, securing their place in the final and marking Marink Reedijk's first win as manager.

The subsequent two victories, 4-0 against Aberdeen and 2-1 against Dundee, have both come in the league, helping Hibernian climb out of the relegation zone and into ninth place.

Hibernian will be looking to build on that improved form with another victory on Saturday, especially as they aim to continue climbing up the table - right now trailing sixth-placed St Johnstone by just three points.

Alongside their recent run, Hibs will draw further confidence from their strength on the road this season, picking up 10 of their 14 points when playing away from home.

Conor Coady has emerged as one of the candidates to become fresh head coach at Blackpool.

The struggling League One side are looking for a latest manager after firing Ian Evatt on his birthday last week.

The Tangerines are understood to have been inundated with applications with the likes of Conor Hourihane, who left Leicester City as assistant manager earlier this month, Matt Bloomfield, formerly Oxford United boss, and Richie Wellens of Leyton Orient among the leading names in the frame.

The 33-year-old retired from playing on November 6 after stints with Wrexham and Charlton Athletic and took up a role as assistant to Lee Carsley in the England U21 set-up in September, replacing Ashley Cole.

Coady had also been helping out within his first club Liverpool's U21 set-up, prior to his deadline day departure from Wrexham.

He is keen to make the step up in club coaching and was linked with a role at Barnsley in recent weeks.

Process of Elimination

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through.
  • Industry observers note that arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight.
  • In hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Piero Hincapie are all reportedly on the verge of fresh deals, with Riccardo Calafiori’s deal also in the in-tray for Andrea Berta too.

Industry observers note that arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight. Back in the summer of 2021, the club enacted a policy of buying players under 24 years old. I always felt like this was the true year zero of the Arteta project. That always felt like the window that built the foundations.

In hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since. Emile Smith Rowe also signed a new contract and took the number 10 shirt that summer and now he is scratching around for minutes at Fulham.

Sources indicate that the summer of 2022 saw the arrivals of Gabriel Jesus and Alex Zinchenko, as well as Fabio Vieira. The former pair briefly elevated Arsenal to a new level before becoming promptly obsolete. Vieira was a fairly pricey gamble that didn’t pay off. It was the summer of 2023 that truly established Arsenal among England’s elite. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Kai Havertz’s arrivals turned Arsenal from caterpillars to butterflies.

Sources indicate that three of those players are about to sign latest contracts. Curiously, we have little to no reporting on whether Kai Havertz is lined up for a new deal as yet. Arsenal are banking on their well assembled core to deliver more silverware as they enter their peak years (Raya is 31 which feels close to peak age for a goalkeeper).

Undoubtedly, there are some players who will drift away in the coming years. Mikel Merino, Martin Zubimendi and Ben White feel unlikely to get newly introduced Arsenal contracts at this particular moment in time. (Though these things can and do change). Like Havertz, Odegaard’s deal runs until the summer of 2028 and we have yet to hear rumblings of a new deal.

It has been revealed that odegaard and Havertz have negotiated significant fitness challenges over the last two seasons, which probably explains why they have found themselves lower down Berta’s to do list. Timber has had his own physical challenges too, but he is 25. Havertz and Odegaard are 27. Their next contracts will be their last ‘big’ contracts in terms of wages and their resale value will drop to close to zero if Arsenal tie them down. It makes sense for the club to take its time a little more with both players.

Both are also defining attacking and / or creative players in the Arsenal team. At some point, Arteta is going to have to plot an evolution within this core and it feels like that is more likely to happen in the final third of the pitch than within the core of players who operate behind the ball. Behind the ball, Arsenal are absolutely tip top and have some of the most elite players in the world in their positions.

That is not as true ahead of the ball. Odegaard and Havertz remain, for my money, elite, defining players for Arsenal. For the purposes of this piece; I am going to speculate that Odegaard is going to be offered a newly introduced contract given his status in the team and because his role is a little more holistic and he doesn’t solely operate in the final third.

Which leaves us with Havertz. I rate Havertz really highly and believe he is integral to Arsenal’s style, he has the technical quality to play one touch football and the physical quality to act as a release valve and hold the ball up. I can’t think of many forwards who offer both sides of the game to such an extent.

Sources indicate that there are several Arsenal attackers I would trade in before Havertz. However, the market doesn’t always bend to your will. Arsenal remain a self sustaining club and in the PSR / SCR era, player trading has never been more important or more voluminous. Keeping money swishing between the cost and revenue columns is a necessity in this environment.

Recent findings suggest that clearly, the number one impediment to Havertz getting a upcoming deal is his fitness. He is still clearly preferred by the manager to Viktor Gyokeres. I have to say I am surprised (a little unpleasantly) at how swiftly the tide of opinion has turned against Havertz. The run he went on very recently that saw him score in the Champions League Final, score the goal that clinched the title against Burnley, a critical goal against Chelsea and the winning goal at Anfield seem to have just bought him absolutely no credit within the fan base, which I find a little surprising.

However, Arsenal need to boost their attacking prowess overall at some point very soon. Like I mentioned, I would consider Havertz a superior player to all of Eze, Gyokeres, Tzolis and Madueke. The squad is well served for numbers in attack; it doesn’t have any gaps in that respect. It has a gap in elite quality.

Sources indicate that the key to boosting that might not be ‘who is the least effective player?’ it might be ‘who is the most saleable?’ Sometimes you do just have to cash in your chips on a player to evolve and move forwards. It doesn’t always have to be because the player is obsolete or not good enough. Arsenal have such numbers in midfield that there also isn’t really a route into the team there for Havertz either.

If someone offered £60-70m for Gyokeres or Eze, I would accept it and give Havertz a latest contract the next day (assuming he does prove his fitness). But I think those scenarios are unlikely. I am not arguing that we have definitely reached the ‘we must sell Kai’ stage and I will reiterate that, at this moment in time, I consider him a very key player who should pretty much always start when fit.

In a recent development, while he isn’t the most prolific finisher as a centre-forward, crucial goals this season against Chelsea and Liverpool demonstrate his worth. The conversation about moving on only becomes live on condition that the money is used to immediately buy an obviously elite attacker- preferably a centre-forward in that case since that is the gap a Havertz departure would leave.

Recent findings suggest that but I am certain it is a conversation Arteta and Andrea Berta are presently entertaining. Arteta will want to push the level of the team even further and, to fund what that is going to entail, potentially painful sales will have to be made somewhere. The vigour with which the club pursued the sale of Gabriel Martinelli this summer reveals the manager has the stomach for that conversation too.

Recent findings suggest that milan go into tonight’s game against Olympiacos needing a win in order to start putting things right in a competition in which they have so far lost three out of four. The top eight expectation has now vanished, with even a play-off spot in jeopardy.

La Gazzetta dello Sport write that Amorim has been coaching two teams since the summer: one which is excellent in the league with some ups and downs, and another that is frankly terrible when the Europa League anthem players.

In a recent development, milan score 2.33 goals per game in the league on average, compared to just 1 per game in Europe. All four of those goals in the UEL came in the win over RB Salzburg too: they have drawn a blank in the other three.

Recent findings suggest that looking a bit deeper, Milan have less possession in Europa League matches (53%, compared to 59% in the league) but shoot 12.5 times per game, more than in Serie A. In Europe they get into the box more often: 26 touches in the opponent’s box compared to 23.

So, why do they score so much less despite being more threatening? Simply put, they shoot worse: the Rossoneri have a very high conversion rate in Serie A (26.4%) which plummets to 10% in Europe. This means that in the UEL it takes 10 shots to score a goal, while in the league it only takes four.

Industry observers note that it’s not all mathematics. Anyone who has watched Milan in Europe have noticed their difficulties. At Bournemouth, they were never in the game, against Ferencvaros they collapsed, against Benfica they deserved to lose against a fellow contender.

Recent findings suggest that with just hours to go before the match against the best defence in the competition, another test awaits. However, Amorim must find a way to concede less too. In Europe, Milan concede 1.92 xG per game, while in the league it’s just 1.28.

This all leads to a discussion about line-ups, and Amorim has rotated a lot outside of league action. The right defender has always been Filippo Terracciano or Fikayo Tomori, never Mario Gila. Without the Spaniard, there’s a noticeable difference.

In midfield, Luka Modric has never started, and Adrien Rabiot started only against Salzburg and Ferencvaros. Up front, Diego Moreira started only against Bournemouth. Life, with or without those three, changes completely.

Amorim already knows he won’t have Modric against Olympiacos, but he can plan with Rabiot and Moreira, concocting a strong side despite the injury complications. He’ll ask for overtime tonight and on Monday in Cagliari, knowing his side will then have almost a week to rest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he debuted a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

ATLETICO ARE AHEAD IN JUST 53 SECONDS! ⚡️ A nightmare start for United at the Metropolitano Stadium 😬 https://t.co/TdOwoXxopn.

They certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Recent findings suggest that ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a big game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC.

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

On the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30.

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

According to recent reports, martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

It has been revealed that no one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring challenges to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Recent findings suggest that having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

Recent findings suggest that it now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

Recent findings suggest that that Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

This feels a massive moment for Carrick and United’s players to answer some of their critics. They have been getting battered from all sides in the last couple of days. Nicky Butt suggested on his podcast that Carrick told him before he got the United job that management “not for me” and “my head’s all over the shop” and that United was the only job he would take. At the very least, those comments are unhelpful and they are thought to have been dimly received internally.

It has been revealed that jamie Carragher offered a lacerating analysis of United’s performance against Spurs on Saturday on Sky Sports on Monday night and suggested things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved if there is not marked improvement. Steven Gerrard questioned why United opted to invest £50m of their summer budget in Andrey Santos, an unused substitute in the last three league games, insisted the back four was not good enough and questioned the work ethic.

And it was interesting to see Carrick alongside his mate Wayne Rooney just now pitchside. Rooney told the Stick to United podcast that captain Bruno Fernandes looks “fed up” and ready to explode at any moment.

It would have been pretty unthinkable for Carrick not to run with a three-man midfield here, not just because of the wide open spaces opponents have exploited this season but when you look at the back line United are fielding. Dalot at left back, two youngsters in Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven and a horribly out of form Lisandro Maríinez.

Recent findings suggest that nor has Senne Lammens looked convincing this term. Matheus Cunha has been dropped – not before time – and I expect to see Fernandes playing off the right. There’s going to a major onus on Rashford on the left. I’m not sure if he is fully fit but he’s going to be crucial.

It’s fantastic. It’s where we want to be, these games, these competitions. It’s as tough a place as you can come to. They’ve got a really good history in this competition and it’s where we want to come to challenge and test ourselves. We have put ourselves in this position, got a good start at home and now this is our first away game.

We want a reaction, of course. A positive reaction [to Saturday’s poor performance]. It hasn’t gone how we wanted, how we expected so far but it’s been fine margins in some of those games. It can go both ways but the reality is where we are at now.

It’s a fresh night and we’ve got to adapt, we’ve got to adjust in a positive way.

We want a little more control in the game [with three central midfielders]. At times we have been too open. We wanted to make a difference in that way. We’ve made other changes, certain spaces, certain positions.

To be honest it’s not really a big change of shape, personnel maybe but a lot of it is similar. We want more control, a little bit without the ball and a lot more with it. We’re happy with the way we set up.

Look at the last three goals we’ve conceded. They’re a mixed bag, simple goals you can something about. We need to defend better as a whole team .

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

Industry observers note that they seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

It has been revealed that the one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Sam Varley | 26 Nov 2026 16:40, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 16:42.

An vital game at the bottom end of the League One table will take place at the Cherry Red Records Stadium on Saturday, as AFC Wimbledon welcome Barnsley.

The hosts sit 18th but only lead the drop zone by three points while their visitors are rooted to the foot of the division and in the midst of a losing run.

AFC Wimbledon are back in League One action on Saturday in search of a second straight home victory to extend their lead over the relegation zone.

The Dons enjoyed a positive start to their second straight campaign in the third tier, earning 12 points from their first eight outings, but they were quickly dragged towards the bottom end of the division, losing four and drawing one of the next five matches.

They scored just three goals in those matches and currently have a league-low tally of 11 goals from 18 games, albeit they were able to make a crucial return to winning ways at home to Blackpool in mid-November, as Alistair Smith's early goal made the only difference.

Johnnie Jackson's men were unable to build on that last time out, though, visiting Leyton Orient and losing 4-1 having trailed by three at the break and pulled one back through Harry Cornick only for Alex Gilbert to put the game out of sight 20 minutes from time.

Now sat 18th, just three points and two places above the bottom four, and with just one league win on the board since mid-September, AFC Wimbledon will again bid to bounce back on Saturday and move further clear of the drop zone and towards mid-table.

Their visitors, meanwhile, head south aiming to arrest a bigger slump which has seen them cut adrift at the bottom of the table.

Daniel Stendel's return to the Barnsley dugout for the 2026-27 season has not gone to plan thus far, as the Yorkshire outfit sit bottom of League One on just nine points from 15 games having won just two and lost 10 of those.

One of those wins and six defeats have come from the Reds' eight away league games thus far, conceding 16 goals in those, while Stendel's men are winless in 11 third-tier outings since early September including three straight defeats heading into the weekend and seven in their last eight.

Following 2-1 losses to Wigan Athletic and South Yorkshire rivals Sheffield Wednesday, they visited Bradford City on Tuesday and suffered a 3-0 beating as Stephen Humphrys scored a brace and Jake Beesley added a late third.

Now rooted to the bottom of the league, four points behind the four teams above them, Barnsley will be desperate to end their long wait for a victory on Saturday and begin climbing towards safety after their dismal start.

AFC Wimbledon form (all competitions):.

Barnsley form (all competitions):.

AFC Wimbledon remain without forward Mathew Stevens due to a long-term injury, while Dujuan Richards and Dan Sweeney are also sidelined.

Attacker Jayden Stockley is back in contention, though, after a suspension last time out, and he will return up front having scored six of the Dons' 11 league goals so far this season.

Cornick will hope to join him, having scored in Stockley's absence at the weekend, with Miles Hippolyte also hoping to continue in an attacking role.

Barnsley are unable to call on attackers Amani Richards, Fabio Jalo and Tobi Adeyemo on Saturday.

Stendel may make changes from the midweek 3-0 loss, with Jubril Okedina in line to return to the defence and Daniel Johnson an option to join Luca Connell in midfield.

That would allow top scorer and captain Cameron McGeehan to return to an advanced midfield role, where he, Reyes Cleary and Vimal Yoganathan may support a lone striker.

AFC Wimbledon possible starting lineup:.

Bishop; Sessegnon, Ogundere, Johnson, Seddon; Nelson, Maycock, Browne; Cornick, Stockley, Hippolyte.

Barnsley possible starting lineup:.

Slicker; Okedina, Kay, Gale, Larkeche; Johnson, Connell; Yoganathan, McGeehan, Cleary; Kirk.

Both teams will see Saturday's game as a significant opportunity to begin turning their form around and it could be a crucial one between the division's worst attack and its second-worst defence and most out-of-form team.

Barnsley look totally devoid of confidence, though, while AFC Wimbledon were able to get the better of Blackpool when they last met fellow strugglers, making them favourites with the best football betting sites, and we give an edge to the hosts as a result.

Mikel Arteta’s press conference takes place early this morning, rather than the typical 1.30pm start time. I woke up a bit later than usual, and there’s part of me that wonders if I should wait for it before doing the blog, but then that would make the blog a lot later than usual and I don’t want to disrupt anybody’s routine. Especially on a Friday.

It has been revealed that so, the talking points will come later, if there are any talking points. My guesses on questions today:.

Also, the bloke from Sky Sports will come to the press conference dressed up as a PS5 controller to ask if the manager is concerned about his players staying up all night to to play Grand Theft Auto 6. Hopefully he requires a firmware enhancement before speaking.

It has been revealed that so, in the absence of news and stuff to talk about, I thought I’d point you in the direction of some stuff elsewhere. In a week where we’ve been handing out upcoming contracts all over the place, Phil Costa wonders about the future of Kai Havertz and whether new terms might be on offer for him.

It’s an interesting one because I think it’s clear he’s the manager’s first preference from the two strikers he has available to him. If he was forced to drive deep into the woods and leave one tied to a tree, it’d be Viktor Gyokeres left in the dark forest to try and undo his knots and make his way back to civilisation. But reservations about Kai’s fitness are more than understandable, and while this is a player who has scored big goals for this club since his arrival, there are inconsistencies to his game that can be frustrating.

It has been revealed that he turns 28 in June, which is far from over the hill, but it’s then about the cost of a multi-year commitment to a player who, more than likely, you’re probably never going to get much of a return on. Particularly if you have to add to what is already a significant weekly wage packet, even if others will have taken over the mantle of Arsenal’s best-paid player.

My gut feeling is that we’ll probably keep him though, and jokes aside it probably is connected to Gyokeres. The Swedish international feels like the player most expendable of the two in the manager’s mind, and I just can’t really see any scenario when simply Arsenal hang onto both for another season or two, or decide that both can be sold and then replaced at the same time. We sold two left-wingers and a striker this summer and replaced them with one single player, so it’s not as if our track record of augmenting the squad in forward areas would give you much confidence in our ability to undergo sweeping reform.

Recent findings suggest that thus, some consistency will be necessary, and if push comes to shove, Arteta will sell Gyokeres a hundred times before Havertz once – unless there’s something to do with fitness/injury. The question then is do we renew now, or see where we are next summer? If we add a younger striker to the mix, the benefit of Havertz’s experience isn’t to be underestimated, and then in those final 12 months, if there’s a deal to be done it can be done, and if not, the club have time to consider other options. At that point, he’ll be almost 29, he’ll have options elsewhere if there’s no future at Arsenal.

Of course players want some security when it comes to their contracts and their futures, it might be a case he wants that and that may force the issue one way or the other, but as it stands, it doesn’t seem to be an issue that absolutely has to be a top priority right now (unlike someone like Declan Rice, for example).

For more good reading this morning, Lewis writes about Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino (the major lumpy prick), and the challenges they face with their newly introduced clubs. I know I mentioned this on the Arsecast Extra earlier in the week, but I really feel like the latter escapes the scrutiny he deserves for the evil he has perpetrated throughout his career. Manager of Sp*rs, Chelsea and PSG, and now Man Utd, as well as a stint as a national manager during which I thought he thoroughly shamed himself over the Folarin Balogun incident in the World Cup. I know he’s a big mate of Mikel Arteta, but for me he’s up there with the worst of them. A Maroon5 cover of a Phil Collins song brought to life.

Recent findings suggest that right, I’ll leave it there. As I remarked yesterday, we’ll have a preview podcast over on Patreon later on, but in the absence of an Arsecast this week we’ll make it available to everyone for free via the usual podcast channels. That should be out after lunch at some time.

💡 Key Takeaways
