💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gleison Bremer's equaliser earned Juventus a point at the Stadio Artemio Franchi after they twice fell behind against Fiorentina.
  • The point leaves Fiorentina 15th in the table on 9 points.
  • According to recent reports, the hosts led after four minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gleison Bremer's equaliser earned Juventus a point at the Stadio Artemio Franchi after they twice fell behind against Fiorentina. Spalletti's side now go into the international break outside the Champions League places, with their next home game brought forward by a day.

The point leaves Fiorentina 15th in the table on 9 points.

According to recent reports, the hosts led after four minutes. Mateo Pellegrino scored, set up by Pedro Goncalves. Nick Woltemade levelled in the 32nd minute from a Randal Kolo Muani assist, and it was 1-1 at half-time.

Fiorentina went ahead again in the 54th minute. Guglielmo Vicario made the first save, but the Juventus defenders were too slow to clear. Alieu Njie forced in the rebound. Bremer then reached a Douglas Luiz corner in the six-yard box before David de Gea could get to it.

Juventus completed 384 accurate passes to Fiorentina’s 273. Fiorentina still attempted 22 shots to Juventus’s 18, and both sides had 6 on target. The expected goals figures, 2.46 for Juventus and 2.14 for Fiorentina, are consistent with a fairly even contest despite the visitors’ control of the ball.

The closing stages could have gone either way. Former Juventus defender Radu Drăgușin headed in from a corner in the 82nd minute. The goal was ruled out because he pushed Bremer with both hands. Near the end, Vicario saved twice in quick succession to protect the point. Juventus also claimed a penalty when the ball struck João Mário’s arm in the Fiorentina area, but none was given.

It has been revealed that referee Andrea Colombo booked three Juventus players. Juan Cabal was cautioned in the 13th minute and Bremer in the 22nd. Kolo Muani was booked for dissent in the 73rd. Christ Inao Oulaï was Fiorentina’s only booking.

Industry observers note that juventus were without the injured Kenan Yildiz, Andrea Cambiaso, Nico González, Manuel Locatelli, Khéphren Thuram and Kamil Grabara. Weston McKennie and Zeki Çelik returned to the squad. Spalletti made three changes in the 57th minute, sending on Zhegrova for Woltemade, Alajbegovic for Boga and Celik for Cabal. Ekhator replaced McKennie in the 78th minute and Gatti came on for Lucumí in the 89th.

At his press conference at the Franchi, Spalletti noted he was not happy because his team does not play at a steady enough level to aim for anything key. He did praise Kolo Muani, describing him as the player everyone wanted and one he can use as a centre-forward or out wide. Shown a replay of the João Mário incident, he dodged the question and asked, smiling, for a different one.

— JuventusFC (@juventusfc) November 8, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the draw ended a run of two wins, against AZ Alkmaar and Napoli. Woltemade and Pellegrino both received a rating of 8.2 from the data provider.

Next up for Juventus is Venezia, who sit 19th on 6 points. When fixture times were first set, that game was pencilled in for Monday 23 November at 20:45 Italian time.

Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.
  • For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.
  • This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

It has been revealed that “Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”.

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso mentioned: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

In a recent development, “We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”.

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

According to recent reports, how different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

Neto fires past Pickford to double Chelsea's lead! 🔥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SOJeBP5mq0.

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

According to recent reports, already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

According to recent reports, chelsea break the deadlock inside a minute of the second half! ⚡ Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max 📺 https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/E63rtGQnbv.

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

Industry observers note that as much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

Industry observers note that he signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

Rogers’s reprieve changed all that. Inexplicably inconsistent as Tierney was, Chelsea exhibited a steel which thrilled Alonso as much as those games when Cole Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro are in full flow.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly said of his attackers.

Sources indicate that alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s new home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

Thanks for reading along this afternoon.

A good win for Chelsea at Everton, but above all, let’s hope Martinez is back to full health soon.

Moyes accepted that his side had were not good enough.

According to recent reports, he told TNT Sports: “We were a little bit unlucky with the goals. It wasn’t good defending, but it takes a couple of deflections before it gets to Neto. It makes it a relatively easy finish for him.

“The second one was a free-kick which obviously ricochets around, so I think there were parts of the game we did OK, but we didn’t offer enough to create enough, to make enough chances. I can’t think of many, so that is probably the biggest indictment.”.

He had a minor gripe over a first-half tackle that was reviewed, saying, “I think the Morgan Rogers tackle on Jimmy [Garner] could have been questioned.”.

However, given the good start to the season for Everton so far, he does not have too much rancour.

Speaking to TNT Sports after the match, Xabi Alonso gives relatively positive news on Emi Martinez.

He describes the planned tests as “precautionary” and states, “as far as I know, he left the stadium conscious.”.

Neto added more detail to his thoughts on the game.

According to recent reports, on his first goal, he explained how Everton’s defensive approach allowed them to react: “We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”.

He credited his Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, with his calmness in front of goal, adding: “This comes a little bit from the new coach of the national team that claims when you are near to the area you need to pass to the goal, so really happy with that.”.

According to recent reports, with Chelsea now in the Champions League places, Neto was keen to keep up the momentum. He said: “It’s really crucial. We know it’s tough to play away, even at home there are no easy games. We came here with personality, with good intentions to win the match and really happy with the result.”.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

He told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”.

He is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is crucial and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”.

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. We have not got too many players. I am not saying we’re going to win the league, but we want to try to challenge and be around the top teams.”.

That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

According to recent reports, yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

Industry observers note that david Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

Villa Midfielder Has £80m Price Tag For Arsenal: Is He Worth It?

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (420 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Footballtransfertavern

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that arsenal transfer news: Aston Villa do not regard Boubacar Kamara as available, even with Arsenal interested, according to CaughtOffside.
  • Villa have already lost Amadou Onana to a torn ACL suffered at the World Cup, and the Belgian is not expected back until around April.
  • According to recent reports, TBR Football reported in July 2025 that he sat on Arsenal’s long list of midfield targets, and his numbers explain why.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that arsenal transfer news: Aston Villa do not regard Boubacar Kamara as available, even with Arsenal interested, according to CaughtOffside. The report says an offer of around £80m could change that stance, although Villa negotiate from strength because the 26-year-old’s contract runs until 2030.

January looks highly unlikely. Villa have already lost Amadou Onana to a torn ACL suffered at the World Cup, and the Belgian is not expected back until around April. Unai Emery cannot lose a second holding midfielder in the middle of a season. The summer is different. CaughtOffside says Villa could entertain a significant bid then, provided they can reinvest the money in a proper replacement and strengthen the squad around him.

According to recent reports, TBR Football reported in July 2025 that he sat on Arsenal’s long list of midfield targets, and his numbers explain why. Kamara has started all 10 of his Premier League games this season, completing 86.3% of his passes, including 83 line-breaking balls, while making 28 tackles and 40 recoveries. He wins 56% of his duels and can play at centre-back, which would give Mikel Arteta cover in two positions.

The weaknesses are just as clear. He has no goals this season, only three shots and an xG of 0.14, and he has committed 20 fouls and conceded a penalty. He also missed the closing weeks of 2024/25 through injury.

The role he would play is obvious: a ball-playing six next to Declan Rice. Martín Zubimendi occupies it now, and Arsenal lead the league with 27 points from 10 games, six clear of Manchester City, with seven clean sheets.

In a recent development, no, not at that price. Arsenal spent £75m on Bruno Guimarães in August, and Arteta still has Rice, Zubimendi, Mikel Merino, Martin Ødegaard and Myles Lewis-Skelly competing for the same central spaces.

Industry observers note that fotMob values him at €49m, roughly £43m, so Villa would be asking close to double his market value for a player who turns 27 this month and offers little in the final third. Villa’s insistence on reinvesting the fee also hands them the leverage, which means Arsenal would pay a premium on a seller’s timetable.

The only sensible trigger is a departure, perhaps Zubimendi or the 30-year-old Merino, leaving Arsenal short of a proven Premier League six. Kamara is a better holding midfielder than most of the market, but a title-leading side already has that job covered, and £80m would buy cover rather than improvement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 12:29 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:33 EST, 25 November 2026.
  • Even for aficionados of the continental game, the draw for the Europa League this year was likely to cause a degree of puzzlement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 12:29 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:33 EST, 25 November 2026.

Even for aficionados of the continental game, the draw for the Europa League this year was likely to cause a degree of puzzlement.

Industry observers note that while not the only outfit to be making its debut in one of UEFA’s competitions, the name of S.C.U. Torreense rang precious few bells among supporters of clubs with a vested interest in how the cards might fall. And little wonder.

Industry observers note that the Portuguese side are plankton in football’s great ocean. Not only have they never played on this stage before, they haven’t even come close to it.

An extraordinary triumph in the Portuguese Cup final – the Taca de Portugal – against Sporting Lisbon in May was their ticket to this journey. In all likelihood, this European adventure will be their first and their last.

Recent findings suggest that it is, of course, not the done thing for anyone connected with any particular club to express a preference as to who they might be drawn against. But representatives of any one of the 35 other sides present at the Grimaldi Forum in Monaco in late August who claimed they weren’t privately hoping for a match against the men from the small city of Torres Vedras were lying.

Recent findings suggest that never mind Benfica, Porto and Sporting Lisbon, the traditional footballing powerhouses of that nation. In terms of support, stature and history, this outfit are a world removed from the likes of Braga and Vitoria Guimaraes, the perennial challengers to the major three.

Torreense players celebrate their victory over Armenian side Ararat in their last European tie.

Torreense’s place in the food chain is underscored by the fact that they can’t even play European matches in their 2,400-capacity Estadio Manuel Marques home because it doesn’t match UEFA criteria.

For the purposes of the Europa League, their fans, who primarily hail from a place which sits 25 miles north of Lisbon, will have to travel to Leiria, which is 60 miles north of their home.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea transfer news: Birmingham Live reports that Alejandro Garnacho’s future needs resolving, because the winger has not started a match for Aston Villa and a permanent move depends on certain conditions being met. Chelsea sent the 22-year-old to Villa Park on a season-long loan in July, with a reported £43m obligation to buy next summer. Neither club has revealed the trigger, and reports link it to appearances.

The numbers explain the concern. FotMob lists four Premier League outings, all from the bench, without a goal or assist, while Football365 counts only 95 minutes across seven substitute appearances. Football Insider claims Villa are prepared to back out of the deal if his form doesn’t improve.

In a recent development, garnacho’s strengths haven’t changed. His pace, directness and willingness to take on defenders earned a £40m move from Manchester United in 2025. The weakness is end product, and it followed him to London with eight goals in 43 games for Chelsea, only one of them in 24 Premier League appearances. Unai Emery left him out of the squad for the Manchester United game.

Chelsea have no obvious use for him either. Xabi Alonso told him in July that regular football wasn’t guaranteed, and the 3-4-2-1 Alonso favours uses Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer behind João Pedro, with Pedro Neto and Estêvão competing for the wide roles.

It has been revealed that fotMob values him at about €29m (roughly £25m), far below the €71m peak recorded in August 2024, and Manchester United are reportedly entitled to 10 per cent of any future fee. If the clause isn’t triggered, he returns in July 2027 on a contract running to 2032.

Yes, and soon. Chelsea built the deal to protect £43m, but the clause relies on appearances from a manager who isn’t picking him, so the price drops with every unused substitution. The sporting case for a return is thin. Alonso’s system asks wide players to defend as wing-backs, while Garnacho’s value lies in isolating a full-back, and the £117m Rogers signing already covers the left-sided attacking role.

In a recent development, A mid-£20m sale, even after United’s cut, would still return more than half of the £40m Chelsea paid and clear a contract running to 2032. Chelsea should open talks with Villa in January about a lower fixed fee, or line up other buyers for the summer. A clause that depends on a manager picking a player he has benched was never a safe way to protect £43m.

Tech Report: Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 80 min read (15911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~80 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, highly heritable, polygenic and easily measured, adult height has long been the model trait in human genetics1,2.
  • Industry observers note that although height was described as a heritable trait as early as 18863, its genetic architecture started to emerge only in the late twentieth century when researchers began identifying the genetic causes of Mendelian syndromes with a substantial stature component4,5,6,7.
  • According to recent reports, by contrast, sequencing-based studies of rare variation can directly implicate causal genes by identifying large-effect putative loss-of-function (pLoF) and missense variants9.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, highly heritable, polygenic and easily measured, adult height has long been the model trait in human genetics1,2. Although the landscape of height-associated common genetic variation has been studied extensively2, rare variation remains relatively unexplored1. Here, using rare protein-altering variants in a discovery set of 826,066 exomes, we identify 207 height-associated genes, 98% of which replicate in an additional 624,567 individuals. The rarest and most deleterious class of variation, singleton (frequency < 0.0001%) putative loss-of-function variants, implicated 17 genes with large effects on height ranging from −17cm (ACAN) to +11 cm (FBN1) per allele, 52× larger than the average effect of common height-associated variants and comparable to the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score. Several genes (TET1, DTL and IGF2BP2) have effect sizes that are at least as large as established Mendelian height genes, yet lack documented stature or skeletal growth syndromes, particularly for genes associated with increased height. Our large-scale sequencing study elucidates the genetic architecture and allelic heterogeneity of rare variants in height, providing unique insights into their large effects—often similar to or larger than recognized Mendelian syndromes—and their impact on trait prediction, clinical evaluation, and discovery power to facilitate drug target prioritization.

Industry observers note that although height was described as a heritable trait as early as 18863, its genetic architecture started to emerge only in the late twentieth century when researchers began identifying the genetic causes of Mendelian syndromes with a substantial stature component4,5,6,7. Non-syndromic genetic modulators of height remained unclear until 2007, when genome-wide association studies (GWASs) identified the first common variants associated with height8. Fifteen years later, a GWAS of 5.3 million individuals identified 12,111 independent variants that collectively accounted for 40% of the variance in height across individuals of European descent2. As with other traits, height GWASs predominantly implicated common non-coding variants with modest effects (<1 cm)2, complicating efforts to link associations directly to specific genes and functional mechanisms.

According to recent reports, by contrast, sequencing-based studies of rare variation can directly implicate causal genes by identifying large-effect putative loss-of-function (pLoF) and missense variants9. To systematically assess the contribution of rare coding variation to height, we performed a multiancestry exome sequencing analysis of adult height in 1,450,633 individuals across 12 cohorts (Supplementary Table 1), in which we (1) identified 17 height-associated genes through a burden of singleton pLoFs; (2) identified additional height-associated genes by including nonsynonymous variants up to 1% alternate allele frequency (AAF) and applying non-burden tests that do not assume variant effects act in the same direction; and (3) estimated the impact of rare protein-altering variation on genetic-based height prediction.

It has been revealed that using 826,066 individuals from six cohorts (Supplementary Table 1), we performed three discovery association analyses of adult height: (1) imputed common variants (AAF > 0.01); (2) rare exome variants (AAF ≤ 0.01, alternate allele count (AAC) ≥ 10); and (3) gene-based tests grouping rare coding variants. We used a single unified Bonferroni significance threshold of 1.75 × 10−9 across all three analyses (Methods). For gene-based analyses, we used a gene-wide omnibus statistic, gene-P10, that aggregates evidence across burden tests and two other gene-based tests, variant-level aggregate Cauchy association tests (ACAT-V)11 and optimal sequence kernel association tests (SKAT-O)12 (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1). We used six additional cohorts with 624,567 individuals for replication (Supplementary Table 1) and assessed the impact of rare variants on height prediction using a subset (n = 242,679).

Industry observers note that common variant analysis identified 3,034 conditionally independent height associations (Supplementary Table 2) that collectively explain around 25% of the observed variation in height (Methods and Supplementary Note). We conditioned on these 3,034 common variants to ensure rare variant and gene-based associations were independent of common variant signals (Supplementary Note and Supplementary Fig. 2). We identified 105 rare nonsynonymous variants in 87 genes (median AAF = 2.16 × 10−3; Supplementary Table 3) and 207 genes associated with height (gene-P < 1.75 × 10−9; Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 4). In total, 82 out of the 87 genes with significant rare nonsynonymous variant associations are also among the 207 genes identified through gene-based tests.

According to recent reports, as singleton pLoFs represent the rarest and most deleterious class of variants, we first focused on this subset. Singleton pLoF burden tests identified 17 genes, 11 height decreasing and 6 height increasing, with a mean absolute effect of 8.92 cm per allele (Fig. 1, Table 1 and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6), about 52× larger than the average GWAS variant (\(\overline{|{\beta }_{\mathrm{GWAS}}|}\) = 0.17 cm) and around 44× larger (range 14.4× to 78.3×) when comparing effects per gene (Methods and Supplementary Table 7). Effects ranged from a 16.6-cm decrease in stature for ACAN singleton pLoF carriers to an 11.1-cm increase in stature for FBN1 singleton pLoF carriers. The effect of carrying a singleton pLoF in one of these 17 genes approaches the cumulative effect observed in the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score (PGS) (top 1%, +9.60 cm; bottom 1%, −9.12 cm; Fig. 2a, Methods and Supplementary Tables 8 and 9). These incredibly rare pLoFs, cumulatively carried by fewer than 0.1% of individuals (744 carriers among 826,066 individuals), have a larger impact on height than all but the most extreme combinations of common variants.

In a recent development, a, pLoF burden effect sizes across AAFs for 17 genes identified by a significant burden of singleton pLoFs (Table 1). b, Same genes as in a, with effect sizes from singleton burden tests across variant classes displayed. c, The relationship between AAF, variant class, effect size, and discovery yield for 179 genes identified from burden tests (Supplementary Tables 6 and 10). Inside each point is the number of genes discovered (top) and the absolute mean effect (in centimetres; bottom). Effect sizes were estimated by multiplying β by the s.d. of observed height (about 7.99 cm). All P values are two-sided, calculated by REGENIE in discovery analysis (n = 826,066), and significance assessed using a P-value threshold of 1.75 × 10−9.

Recent findings suggest that a, Percentiles of a height PGS (grey) derived from common variants (AAF > 1%; 3,034 GWAS variants + 5 common exome variants; Supplementary Table 8) representing the mean height difference between replication individuals in each PGS percentile (n = 2,427) compared with the remaining ancestry/sex-matched individuals (n = 240,252; Supplementary Table 9). The coloured points are mean significant burden test effect sizes (split by effect direction) placed for comparison to the PGS. The error bars represent 95% CIs around the mean effect estimated from REGENIE. b, The inverse relationship between effect size (in centimetres; y axis) and AAF (x axis) for burden tests (Supplementary Table 6), exome variants (Supplementary Table 3) and conditionally independent common variants (Supplementary Table 2) from discovery (n = 826,066 individuals). The triangles denote burden tests (with a smaller shape for the burden AAF threshold embedded inside), and the circles denote individual variants. The colour denotes the predicted consequence of individual variants or variants included in the burden test. The full distribution is shown in the inset.

These 17 genes belong to well-established biological processes and pathways affecting height, including extracellular matrix organization and skeletal/growth pathways such as growth hormone/insulin-like growth factor (GH/IGF), WNT/β-catenin and transforming growth factor-β1,13,14,15 (TGFβ) (Table 1 and Extended Data Table 1).

Incorporating more common variation into burden tests can increase statistical power for gene discovery by adding variant carriers, although at the cost of attenuated effect sizes. Expanding our analysis to include increasingly frequent pLoFs, followed by including missense variants, identified an additional 162 genes (Extended Data Fig. 1).

Among pLoFs, relaxing the burden test AAF threshold from singletons (about 0.00006%) to 1% identified 76 genes, 62 not discovered with pLoF singletons alone. On average, burden tests aggregating more common pLoFs had a 3.96-cm effect—less than half the 8.92-cm effect of pLoF singletons, but still 24× larger than the average GWAS association (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 10). Among the 15 genes with pLoF singleton associations that remained significant at AAF < 0.01%, we observed a 35% attenuation in the absolute effect size (from 8.71 cm to 5.68 cm), suggesting that a substantial fraction of more frequent pLoF-annotated variants may not cause complete loss of function. Two genes—CHD8 (associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability) and COL1A1 (associated with Ehlers–Danlos syndrome16 and osteogenesis imperfecta)—were identified only through singleton pLoF burden tests. When more frequent pLoFs were included, burden test effect sizes fell by 78% for COL1A1 and 83% for CHD8 and were no longer statistically significant (Fig. 1a). By contrast, three genes with absolute effects on height of >1 s.d. (7.99 cm) reached significance only with higher-frequency pLoFs: SHOX17 in the fibroblast growth factor pathway (β = −12.05 cm, P = 2.85 × 10−16); transcriptional regulator ERF (β = −8.67 cm, P = 4.41 × 10−21); and HMGA2, the insulin-like growth factor pathway gene underlying the first height GWAS discovery8 (β = −8.11 cm, P = 6.11 × 10−13). These three genes each had few singleton pLoFs (1, 6, and 16 carriers, respectively); aggregating singletons with additional rare pLoFs was therefore essential to achieve significance.

This expanded set of height-associated pLoF burden genes highlighted additional canonical growth pathways and height biology (for example, the fibroblast growth factor pathway; Extended Data Table 1), as well as additional members from the same gene families and pathways implicated by pLoF singleton genes (Supplementary Table 11).

Whereas pLoFs represent the rarest and most deleterious class of coding variation, missense variants represent the most frequent class of protein-altering variants9,18,19. If missense variants ablate protein function to a similar extent as pLoFs, we might expect both increased statistical power and similar effect sizes when combining both in burden tests. Conversely, if missense variants only partially diminish protein function or exert opposing effects through gain-of-function (GoF) mechanisms, burden effect sizes will be attenuated.

It has been revealed that we combined pLoFs with three sets of missense variants: (1) all missense variants; (2) missense variants inconsistently classified as deleterious by in silico algorithms (possibly deleterious); and (3) missense variants confidently classified as deleterious by in silico algorithms (deleterious; Methods), collectively identifying 154 genes (85 not discovered by pLoFs alone; Fig. 1c). When combined with pLoF variants, successively filtering rare missense variants for increasing deleteriousness increased discovery power, yielding 96, 116, and 132 genes for each of the above groups, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

Among the 14 genes with both significant singleton pLoF and singleton pLoF + deleterious missense burden associations (Table 1), the absolute effect size decreased 28.5% on average when adding deleterious missense singletons (8.70 cm versus 6.22 cm; Fig. 1b). This observation holds broadly across height-associated genes, with diminished pLoF + missense effect sizes reflecting both that missense variants account for most rare allele carriers (68.5% in singleton and 84.1% in AAF < 1% burden tests) and that the effect of missense variants is, on average, substantially smaller than that of pLoFs (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 10). Despite diminished effect sizes, the higher allele counts contributed by missense variants substantially increased overall discovery power, more than doubling the number of associated height genes.

Of the 85 genes not discovered by pLoFs alone, UHRF2 (singleton pLoF + deleterious missense variants: β = −4.74 cm, P = 3.6 × 10−12)—an E3 ubiquitin ligase regulating the cell cycle20—and PTPN11 (pLoF + deleterious missense variants AAF < 0.01%: β = −4.00 cm, P = 2.5 × 10−32)—a signalling protein involved in development and hormone response through the RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT signalling pathways21—had the largest effect sizes.

We found six genes (ESR1, FGFR3, HSD11B2, MTMR11, PTPN11 and RPL5) that exhibited the strongest association from missense-only burden tests, and pLoF burden tests were, at best, only nominally significant (Supplementary Table 13). Four genes (FGFR3, HSD11B2, PTPN11 and RPL5) had opposite directions of effect between pLoF and missense burden tests, although the pLoF estimates were not statistically significant. Notably, three genes—FGFR3 (refs. 7,22), PTPN11 (ref. 23) and ESR1 (ref. 24)—have previously reported GoF mutations that drive syndromic conditions with notable skeletal growth phenotypes, including achondroplasia (FGFR3)22 and Noonan syndrome (PTPN11)23. Given the known GoF mechanisms for three of these genes, the other missense-driven genes may also affect height through GoF mechanisms.

The newly introduced genes identified by incorporating missense variants further underscore previously implicated pathways, biological functions and gene families (Supplementary Table 11) but also implicate different pathways (for example, Sonic Hedgehog signalling) and biological processes, including sex hormone regulation and carbohydrate transport, storage and metabolism (Extended Data Table 1).

It has been revealed that although burden tests identified 179 height-associated genes (Extended Data Fig. 1a), they were not designed to identify genes of which variants with effects exist in opposite directions or where most variants have no effect. For these situations, SKAT-O12 and ACAT-V11 were developed.

Recent findings suggest that collectively, ACAT-V and SKAT-O identified 28 genes not detected by burden tests (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Before conditional analysis, ACAT-V and SKAT-O associations were more likely than burden test associations to be driven by linkage disequilibrium with common variants (Supplementary Note, Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 12). Consistent with the underlying model, SKAT-O associations highlight genes harbouring variants with opposing effects on height. For example, in PTCH1, a transmembrane protein receptor involved in Hedgehog signalling25, the SKAT-O association (P = 1.94 × 10−15) was driven by two variants: a missense variant associated with increased height (9:95458026G>A; p.T1052M; β = +1.00 cm, P = 4.8 × 10−11; Supplementary Table 3) and a splice acceptor variant associated with decreased height (9:95485875C>T; β = −4.28 cm, P = 1.9 × 10−9). Meanwhile, ACAT-V identified genes like FBN2 (P = 1.72 × 10−12), a component of microfibrils that stores and regulates growth factors including TGFβ26, in which the association was driven by one significant missense variant (5:128332993G>T; p.H1381N; β = +1.07 cm, P = 9.8 × 10−14; AAF = 0.48%; Supplementary Table 3).

Although gene-based tests are useful for boosting rare variant discovery power, we identified 121 significant rare (AAF < 1%) exome variants after conditioning on common GWAS variants (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Tables 3 and 14 and Supplementary Note). Of these 121 variants, 105 were nonsynonymous (85 missense, 17 pLoFs and 3 in-frame insertions or deletions (indels)) and implicated 87 genes, 82 of which overlapped genes implicated by gene-based tests (60 from burden tests; 22 genes from ACAT-V or SKAT-O).

For the 82 genes identified by both single variants and gene-based tests, we compared the consistency of effect sizes between burden test and significant individual variants (Methods). Focusing on the 79 rare nonsynonymous variants (59 missense, 17 pLoFs, 3 in-frame indels) in 60 genes with a significant burden test, we found that 52 (66%) had larger effect sizes than the largest burden test effect. The neurodevelopmental-disorder-associated gene KMT2B27 had the largest discrepancy, with a nearly 20-fold difference between variant 19:35720959C>T (p.R538C; β = −7.67 cm, P = 2.6 × 10−10, AAF = 2.61 × 10−5) and the largest burden test effect (β = −0.38 cm, P = 5.0×10−10; pLoF and possibly deleterious missense variants with AAF < 0.01%).

Two genes with GoF missense variants, FGFR3 and PTPN11, have multiple missense variants with some of the largest observed effects on height (Fig. 2b). Among the six exome-wide significant variants in FGFR3, a pathogenic GoF missense variant causing achondroplasia7 (4:1804392G>A; p.G380R; P = 3.22 × 10−64) decreases height by 29.78 cm, about 13× larger than the largest FGFR3 burden test effect (β = −2.31 cm, P = 2 × 10−41; deleterious missense variants AAF < 0.0001; Extended Data Fig. 2). PTPN11 also contains two significant pathogenic GoF missense variants23,28: p.R265Q (12:112472981G>A; β = −12.26 cm, P = 6 × 10−19) and p.N308D (12:112477719A>G; β = −14.21 cm, P = 4 × 10−14), with effects around 3× larger than the largest burden signal (β = −4.12 cm, P = 3.6 × 10−33; deleterious missense variants with AAF < 0.0001). These examples emphasize the challenge that allelic heterogeneity presents for interpreting and using gene-level burden effect sizes. We discuss the implications of effect size heterogeneity on phenotypic prediction below (see the ‘Heritability, enrichment and prediction’ section).

Sources indicate that recent studies29,30 demonstrated that non-additive models can identify associations missed by standard approaches; we therefore tested rare coding variants under a recessive model. This identified only one association missed by additive tests: the CFTR ΔF508 mutation that causes cystic fibrosis31 was not associated with height under an additive model (βadd = −0.05 cm; Padd = 0.14), but was associated with a 5.87-cm height reduction in homozygotes in the recessive model (Prec = 5 × 10−10; replication and additional details are provided in the Supplementary Note). This result is consistent with both the recessive nature of cystic fibrosis mutations and the established impact of cystic fibrosis on growth and stature. The inability of cystic fibrosis treatments to fully restore growth trajectory and stature, along with diminished IGF1 levels exhibited by newborns with cystic fibrosis, are findings compatible with a direct effect of CFTR on height through fetal and/or neonatal growth pathways32,33.

Industry observers note that we sought to understand the differences in genetic architecture across genetic ancestry groups by stratifying single-variant and gene-based tests by ancestry (Methods). Consistent with previous findings, we detected no effect-size heterogeneity by genetic ancestry34. However, we identified several ancestry-specific signals resulting from differences in AAF and sample size. Most associations specific to a single ancestry were identified in the European subset, which accounts for most participants (n = 640,240, 78%; Supplementary Table 15 and Supplementary Note). One notable exception is a rare HHIP p.V496E substitution associated with decreased height exclusively in the admixed American subpopulation (AMR AAF = 0.05%, P = 1.52 × 10−9, β = −3.96 cm; Supplementary Table 15 and Supplementary Note). This variant is observed only in individuals from the Mexico City Prospective Study35. We speculate that the p.V496E variant is a GoF missense variant, as rare HHIP pLoFs appear to be associated with increased height (pLoF singleton β = +9.92 cm, P = 3.72 × 10−7). Similarly, we replicate a known signal at a FBN1 missense variant36 (p.E1297G; β = −2.12 cm, P = 2.9 × 10−17; Supplementary Table 16) that is substantially more common in admixed Americans (about 1% versus 0.004% in Europeans) and occurs almost exclusively on Indigenous haplotypes (Supplementary Fig. 4). These discoveries underscore the value of sequencing diverse populations.

Industry observers note that height GWASs14 have consistently observed enrichment of Mendelian syndrome genes among height-associated common variant loci37; we observed similar enrichment in genes implicated through rare variation. Forty-three out of 76 genes (57%) with significant pLoF burden signals at AAF < 1% and 102 out of 207 (49%) height-associated genes in total were documented in the Mendelian syndrome in Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database, significantly more than expected by chance (odds ratio (OR) = 4.46, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 2.76–7.26, P = 1.83 × 10−10; Fisher’s exact test). Of the 43 Mendelian genes, 21 had annotated stature or skeletal growth features2, an 8.37-fold enrichment (95% CI = 4.34–16.10, P = 2.56 × 10−10; Fisher’s exact test). Genes with pLoF burden height associations and a Mendelian syndrome listed in OMIM are over 5× more likely to be associated with decreased height (36 out of 43, 83%). Among the 11 pLoF singleton genes with height-decreasing effects, 9 were in OMIM and 8 list stature or skeletal growth among the clinical characteristics. By contrast, among the six with height-increasing effects, three are in OMIM, but only FBN1 includes height among the clinical characteristics. Our results were insufficient to determine whether increased height is under-reported as a syndromic feature or whether genes leading to increased height are less likely to cause other clinical features and therefore cause fewer recognized syndromes (Supplementary Note).

Previous studies estimated that the gene nearest to a GWAS peak is the causal gene in around 70% of instances9,38. We observed strong overlap between large-effect rare variant burden associations and GWAS peaks, although this overlap diminishes noticeably with the stringency of the burden definition and variant frequency. Of pLoF singleton genes, 82% (14 out of 17) are the closest gene to a GWAS peak, compared with only 60% (92 out of 154) of pLoF + missense burden genes. In total, 28 out of 207 genes are not among the top 10 nearest genes to any common variant signal. Notably, 4 genes are >1 Mb from the nearest common variant association signal: FIBIN, HHIPL1, PTPN11 and WLS. Even compared with the 12,111 index variants from ref. 2, PTPN11 is not among the 10 nearest genes to any GWAS peak, with the closest signal 393 kb away (Supplementary Table 4).

Recent findings suggest that to assess the validity of our results, we performed replication analyses in six independent cohorts comprising an additional 624,567 individuals (Supplementary Table 1). Despite the 24.4% smaller sample size, 203 out of 207 (98.1%) genes and 113 out of 125 (90.4%) single variants replicated with nominal significance (α = 0.05; Methods, Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 and Supplementary Note), demonstrating both high consistency of height associations and the robustness of our Bonferroni threshold. Furthermore, replication rates were consistent across gene-based tests—BURDEN-ACAT, 98.1% (155 out of 158); SBAT, 93.8% (166 out of 177); SKAT-O, 95.3% (164 out of 172); and ACAT-V, 94.9% (94 out of 99; Supplementary Fig. 5b–e). Replication performance for single variants improved to 96.1% (98 out of 102) after restricting to variants with over 80% estimated replication power (Supplementary Fig. 5f). Irrespective of power, all 179 burden genes and all but one variant had consistent directions of effect between discovery and replication analyses (Supplementary Note). Furthermore, gene-based tests maintained high replication rates well above our study-wide P-value threshold (Supplementary Note and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). For example, 91.6% of the 368 genes reaching a discovery gene-P < 2.5 × 10−6—roughly equivalent to one test per gene—replicated with nominal significance (P < 0.05) and would implicate an additional 137 genes compared to our experiment-wide Bonferroni threshold (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Replication rates for single variants and singleton burden tests declined similarly, requiring respective P-value thresholds of 4 × 10−6 and 1 × 10−6 to achieve a comparable 91.6% replication rate when restricted to tests with over 80% power (Supplementary Figs. 5f and 6).

It has been revealed that finally, because burden tests were more likely to have negative (height-decreasing) effect estimates, we compared the ratio of effect directions across significance thresholds (Supplementary Note and Extended Data Fig. 3). The excess of height-decreasing burden effects persists well below the Bonferroni significance threshold, with the degree of imbalance varying by both significance threshold and variant class. These patterns suggest considerable rare variant signal yet to be discovered.

Industry observers note that rare variants are frequently offered as an answer to the ‘missing heritability’ problem in complex trait genetics39. Here we estimated the cumulative impact of rare coding variation on height at the population level by calculating the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to burdens of rare coding variants and assessing the potential of large-effect height-associated coding variants to improve height predictions.

First, burden heritability regression40 estimated the burden of rare nonsynonymous variants explain 3.97% (95% CI = 3.77–4.17%) of phenotypic variance (Extended Data Fig. 4, Supplementary Table 17 and Supplementary Note), nearly identical to the previously published estimate of 3.82% (95% CI = 3.55–4.09%)40. pLoFs with AAF < 0.001% accounted for the largest fraction of burden heritability, consistent with the large effects we observed for these extremely rare, damaging variants. This probably underestimates the true contribution of rare coding variants because the burden approach underestimates heritability in the presence of effect size heterogeneity40. Together, the most significant burden test for each of the 179 burden genes explains around 1.1% of phenotypic variance in the replication data, nearly 30% of the total estimated contribution of the burden of rare variants to adult height (Extended Data Fig. 5).

We next tested for enrichment of rare, deleterious variants in individuals whose height was poorly predicted by common variants in our replication data (n = 242,679), as rare variants unaccounted for in common variant prediction may contribute to the discrepancy between observed and genetically predicted height41,42,43. Individuals deviating from their common variant predicted height by >2.5 s.d. (±17–20 cm) were 17.2-fold (95% CI = 9.89–28.34, P = 1.12 × 10−16, Fisher’s exact test) enriched for carrying a singleton pLoF in one of the 17 singleton pLoF genes (Fig. 3a, Methods and Supplementary Table 18). By contrast, individuals at the extreme ends of the height distribution (>2.5 s.d.) were only 4.9-fold enriched (P = 1.89 × 10−7, Fisher’s exact test; Supplementary Table 19 and Supplementary Note) for pLoF singletons in these genes, consistent with previous results42,43.

We next focused on the 337 individuals in the replication data carrying a pLoF singleton in one of the 17 genes with significant pLoF singleton burden (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 5). In these individuals, adding burden effects to a common variant prediction model (Methods) improved the R2 from 0.55 to 0.72 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Note). This brings the performance in line with common variant prediction across the entire replication sample (R2 = 0.73). Including pLoF singleton burden effects into prediction also reduced the s.d. of the error distribution by 1.55 cm, signifying more consistent predictions; however, improvement varied substantially by gene (Fig. 3c,d and Extended Data Fig. 6).

Given the large effects of rare missense variants in FGFR3 and PTPN11 (Fig. 2b), we evaluated the performance of several rare variant-based prediction models compared with standard common variant PGS in these variant carriers (Fig. 3d and Methods). Among 29 carriers of five rare deleterious missense variants in these two genes in the replication dataset, the prediction R2 dropped slightly from 0.158 to 0.155 when adding a PGS built from deleterious missense (AAF < 1%) burden effect sizes (Supplementary Fig. 7). By contrast, the prediction R2 increased to 0.67 when adding a PGS based on individually significant rare variants. This difference in prediction performance was especially pronounced among the six carriers of FGFR3 p.G380R (4:1804392:G:A; βdiscovery = −29.8 cm, P = 3.2 × 10−64; Fig. 2b)—a ClinVar pathogenic variant reported for achondroplasia7 (Fig. 3d))—for whom height prediction improved by an average of 26.1 cm after accounting for the variant. Aggregate burden effects are largely unsuitable in prediction for genes with substantial effect size heterogeneity, such as FGFR3 and PTPN11 (Supplementary Note). Still, individual rare variants are difficult to incorporate in prediction, as variants are frequently not observed in reference samples or effects are estimated from few observations. Overall, we observe that PGSs that supplement common variants with both aggregate rare variant effects and individual rare variants with extreme effects perform best for height prediction (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Finally, population-based data can provide a useful orthogonal resource to aid clinical variant interpretation19. We assessed whether our association results could inform pathogenicity classification of ClinVar variants with conflicting classifications of pathogenicity (CCOPs) or variants of uncertain significance (VUSs). To maximize power for these ultrarare variants, we performed a meta-analysis of our discovery and replication data (Supplementary Tables 20 and 21 and Extended Data Fig. 7) for the 5,233 rare variants in our 207 height-associated genes that were evaluated in ClinVar for links to stature-related syndromes (Methods). In total, 39 variants were significantly associated with height, including 20 VUSs/CCOPs. Of those 20 variants, one—an ADAMTS10 splice region variant—was associated with increased height (β = +2.3 cm, P = 3.9 × 10−15), the opposite direction of ADAMTS10’s burden test effects (Supplementary Table 6). The pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) category contained more significant height-associated variants than expected by chance (P = 6 × 10−12, binomial test), as did the CCOP and benign/likely benign categories (Supplementary Table 22).

Recent findings suggest that we next looked for variants absent from ClinVar with absolute effect sizes greater than 7.99 cm (1 s.d.), an effect size greater than 77% of the stature-related P/LP variants in our 207 genes (Fig. 4). At this effect size threshold, four significant variants were completely absent from ClinVar as of July 2025 (Supplementary Table 21): pLoFs in HMGA2 (p.E98*), LCORL (p.S1370Rfs*10) and ADAMTS17 (p.S971*), and a missense substitution in ZFAT (p.R762C).
