📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 26 Nov 2026 22:46, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 22:47.

Bournemouth have become just the third team to win their first five matches in a major European competition.

The Cherries travelled to Vigo with a perfect record in the competition after beating Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, AC Milan and Sparta Prague.

Their impressive record looked set to end when they went a goal and a man down inside the first quarter at Balaidos.

Bournemouth showed character to recover from Bafode Diakite's red card by staging a dramatic second-half turnaround that started with Alvaro Rodriguez's equaliser.

Rayan then netted a 78th-minute winner to fire the Cherries to a 2-1 victory, sending them into an outright lead at the top of the Europa League league phase with the only 100% record out of the 36 teams.

Not only have they significantly boosted their chances of securing a top-eight finish, but the Cherries also became the third team to win their first five games in European competition.

German side Nurnberg were the first team to achieve the feat on their way to reaching the quarter-finals of the 1961-1962 European Cup.

Armenian side Ararat Yerevan replicated the feat when they won the first five games of their UEFA Cup campaign in 1972-1973 before losing on penalties to Kaiserlautern in the last 16.

As well as joining Nurnberg and Ararat in an exclusive group, Bournemouth also became the first Premier League side in three years to win a competitive game after trailing at half time while being a player down.

Prior to Thursday's win, Liverpool were the last team to achieve that feat when Darwin Nunez netted a late brace in a 2-1 victory after Virgil van Dijk had been sent off in the first period.

After winning 10 consecutive games in all competitions for the first time in their history, Bournemouth will now start preparation for Sunday's Premier League meeting with Fulham at Craven Cottage.

Marco Rose's side will then play two more league games against Brighton & Hove Albion and Hull City before they return to Europa League action against Viktoria Plzen on December 10.

Bournemouth head into the weekend in fifth spot in the Premier League table and just three points adrift of fourth-placed Liverpool.

#209302. Latest Update: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts

Latest Update: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 57 min read (11473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~57 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide1,2,3,4, yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood.
  • Recent findings suggest that shifts in the distribution of tree species in response to climate change1,2 and disturbances3,4 can substantially affect forest structure, biodiversity and ecosystem services5,6,7,8.
  • In a recent development, forests in the western USA span a broad elevational range, from near sea level to approximately 3,700 m, near the upper treeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide1,2,3,4, yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood. Here we analyse repeated measurements from 44,368 forest inventory plots spanning 1999–2025, with an average remeasurement interval of 10 years, to examine how climate and natural disturbances jointly influence the elevational redistribution of tree species across the western USA. We show that climate warming increased sapling abundance, whereas increasing drought frequency and recent natural disturbances (fire, insect outbreaks and disease) reduced tree abundance, particularly among adult trees. By contrast, legacy fire was associated with increased sapling abundance, with stronger positive responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. These influences were distributed unevenly across species’ elevational ranges: upper portions of species’ ranges generally experienced stronger warming, greater increases in drought frequency and more disturbance activity than lower portions, creating elevational asymmetries in stress and recovery. These elevational asymmetries were associated with more pronounced downslope shifts in basal area centres, probably reflecting disturbance effects on larger trees. By contrast, stem abundance centres showed more divergent shifts, consistent with sapling responses to both climate change and disturbance. Our findings reveal contrasting demographic responses to climate change and natural disturbances that shape the elevational redistribution of different species, with potential consequences for forest composition, resilience and long-term stability.

Recent findings suggest that shifts in the distribution of tree species in response to climate change1,2 and disturbances3,4 can substantially affect forest structure, biodiversity and ecosystem services5,6,7,8. Such redistribution can be characterized by shifts in tree abundance centres, which reveals how populations reorganize within their ranges2,9,10. Given that cooler conditions occur at higher latitudes and elevations, poleward and upslope shifts in species distribution are expected with climate change1,9,10,11,12. However, downslope shifts of tree species in montane ecosystems have also been reported, probably reflecting the influence of non-temperature factors that alter tree abundance and distribution in contrasting ways13,14,15,16. Natural disturbances, such as wildfires, diseases and insect outbreaks, along with subsequent regeneration, can alter stem abundance and basal area (the cross-sectional surface area of tree trunks measured at breast height—1.37 m above the ground) across regions4, influencing latitudinal or longitudinal shifts3. Yet, the roles of disturbances in shaping species’ elevational redistribution remains underexplored8.

In a recent development, forests in the western USA span a broad elevational range, from near sea level to approximately 3,700 m, near the upper treeline. Over recent decades, these forests have experienced pronounced warming and frequent droughts17,18, which have increased wildfire activity19,20 and insect outbreaks21,22, and altered forest disease patterns22,23. As these disturbances can alter tree demographic dynamics4, elevational variation in disturbance activity may drive the elevational redistribution of tree abundance. Moreover, warming may shift disturbance patterns23,24,25, further influencing tree abundance redistribution. Although previous studies have reported elevational shifts across regions, most have been restricted geographically with inconsistent patterns9,14,26,27,28. A comprehensive and cross-regional assessment using a consistent methodology remains lacking, which limits our understanding of elevational shift patterns and their underlying mechanisms in the context of environmental change.

To fill this gap, we quantified elevational shifts in tree abundance centres of common tree species across individual ecosections (ecoregion sections) in the western USA using remeasured plots conducted by the US Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) programme29. As the western USA spans a vast climatic and ecological gradient and encompasses diverse forest types, estimating elevational shifts across the entire region would mask regional-scale differences and could be confounded by species’ geographical redistribution among regions14,30,31,32. We therefore conducted our analyses separately within individual ecosections for each species. By selecting tree species that occurred in more than 100 remeasured FIA plots without evidence of silvicultural treatment within individual montane ecosections (Fig. 1a), we identified 45 species (Extended Data Table 1) across 33 ecosections, yielding 212 species–ecosection combinations. Collectively, they accounted for 68% of total stems and 69% of total basal area across montane forests in the western USA.

Industry observers note that a, Map of montane ecoregion provinces and sections. Letters indicate the section code in each ecoregion province. Only ecosections with species represented by more than 100 remeasured plots are shaded. These ecosections occur within the following montane provinces: M242 (Cascade Mixed Forest), M261 (Sierran Steppe), M313 (Arizona–Upcoming Mexico Mountains Steppe), M331 (Southern Rocky Mountain Steppe), M332 (Middle Rocky Mountain Steppe), M333 (Northern Rocky Mountain Forest) and M341 (Nevada–Utah Mountain Steppe). b, Distributions of elevational shifts in basal area (left) and stem abundance (right) of 212 species–ecosections. The proportions of total stems or basal area with significant downslope (brown) and upslope (green) shifts are annotated. c, Mean shift rates in individual ecosections, weighted by basal area (left) and stem abundance (right) across species. Light blue shading is to distinguish ecoregion provinces. d, Mean shift rates for each species, weighted by basal area (left) and stem abundance (right) across ecosections. Light blue shading is to distinguish different genera. Symbol size in c and d denotes relative tree abundance, calculated as the proportion of basal area or stem abundance relative to the total. In b–d, brown and green denote significant (P < 0.05) downslope and upslope shifts, respectively, and grey indicates shifts that are not significant (NS). In d, species are shown in phylogenetic order. Statistical significance of elevational shifts was assessed using two-sided paired bootstrap tests with 10,000 resamples. Scale bar, 500 km.

It has been revealed that in this study, we aimed to address three objectives: (1) to characterize patterns of elevational shifts in tree abundance centres across species–ecosections in the western USA under climate change and natural disturbances; (2) to examine how climate and disturbance jointly influence tree abundance changes and (3) to evaluate how elevational asymmetries in climate and disturbance activity influence the elevational redistribution of tree abundance. We quantified elevational shifts for individual species–ecosections using two measures of tree abundance: basal area and stem abundance. For each measure, the shift was calculated as the difference in species’ elevational centres between two inventory periods (T1, 1999–2013 and T2, 2012–2025), yielding the basal area shift and stem shift. Changes in stem abundance and basal area both reflect demographic processes but differ in their sensitivity to tree size classes. Stem abundance may be influenced more strongly by sapling dynamics (mortality and ingrowth), as saplings are typically more numerous than adult trees. Here, ingrowth refers to the entry of stems into a specified size class by crossing a diameter threshold as defined by the FIA: sapling ingrowth occurs when stems enter the 2.54–12.7 cm diameter at breast height (DBH) class, and adult ingrowth occurs when stems grow beyond 12.7 cm DBH. FIA ingrowth therefore represents the combined outcome of earlier recruitment, survival and growth sufficient for an individual to cross an inventory threshold. Basal area gives greater weight to larger trees and is influenced more strongly by the growth and mortality of adult trees. Thus, the two measures provide complementary information on population change. Because shifts in abundance centre ultimately arise from asymmetric tree abundance changes along species’ elevational gradients, understanding the drivers of plot-level tree abundance change is essential for interpreting the mechanisms underlying these shifts. We then assessed the effects of changes in mean annual temperature (MAT) and drought frequency, together with disturbance factors including fire, insect outbreaks and disease, on plot-level tree abundance changes. Finally, we investigated the elevational asymmetries in these environmental factors, defined as differences between elevational segments above (upper) and below (lower) the elevational centre at T1, and evaluated their associations with ecosection-level elevational shifts using generalized linear mixed models.

In a recent development, elevational redistribution of basal area and stem abundance varied substantially among species–ecosections, with many showing little change in elevational centres whereas others exhibited significant upslope or downslope shifts (Extended Data Fig. 1). For basal area, shifts were more often downslope than upslope: 42 of 212 species–ecosections shifted significantly (P < 0.05) downslope and 28 shifted upslope, representing 30% and 11% of total basal area across all focal species–ecosections, respectively. When aggregating all species within individual ecosections, 12 of the total 33 ecosections shifted downslope, whereas four ecosections shifted upslope (Fig. 1c). Except for the Nevada–Utah Mountain Steppe (M341), downslope shifts were more common than upslope shifts across ecoregion provinces (Fig. 1c). When aggregating across ecosections by species, 16 species (61.5% total basal area) experienced a significant downslope shift and 11 (11.3% total basal area) shifted upslope. Among the eight most dominant species, six shifted downslope (P < 0.05), including Pseudotsuga menziesii (Douglas fir), Pinus ponderosa (ponderosa pine), Pinus contorta (lodgepole pine), Tsuga heterophylla (western hemlock), Picea engelmannii (Engelmann spruce) and Abies concolor (white fir), whereas none shifted upslope (Fig. 1d).

In a recent development, when measured by stem abundance, shift in elevational centre was more divergent. Specifically, 23 species–ecosections moved downslope and 22 upslope (Extended Data Fig. 1), representing 7.4% and 10.7% of total stem abundance across all focal species–ecosections, respectively (Fig. 1b). Spatially, five ecosections exhibited significant overall downslope shifts, whereas six ecosections showed significant upslope shifts (Fig. 1c). At the species level, only three species shifted downslope and six shifted upslope (Fig. 1d), reflecting divergent elevational responses among ecosections within individual species (Extended Data Fig. 1).

To understand demographic changes underlying the observed elevational shifts, we examined range-edge dynamics by comparing relative tree abundance change between the upper and lower range segments for species–ecosections with significant shifts (Extended Data Fig. 2). Upper and lower range segments were defined as portions of a species’ range above and below the elevational centre weighted by basal area or stem abundance from the initial inventory (T1). For basal area, 61% of upslope shifts and 69% of downslope shifts were associated with consistent changes of basal area in upper and lower segments (either both declining or both increasing, but at differing rates above versus below the elevational centre). For stem abundance, 64% of upslope shifts were associated with declines at lower and increases at upper-range segments, whereas 57% of downslope shifts demonstrated the opposite pattern. This indicates that stem shifts are associated with asymmetric demographic responses between cooler (upper) and warmer (lower) elevational segments, with increase in abundance at one end coupled with decline at the other.

Sources indicate that we further analysed the tree abundance change at upper and lower ranges for saplings and adult trees, separately. The asymmetric responses of saplings between range segments aligned with stem-based shifts, whereas those of adults aligned with basal area shifts, indicating that stem shifts were driven primarily by changes in sapling abundance and basal area shifts were driven primarily by changes in adult basal area (Extended Data Fig. 2b). Results were similar when using plots in the uppermost and lowermost 25% of elevations (Supplementary Fig. 1).

In a recent development, as uneven changes in tree abundance along elevational gradients drive shifts in abundance centre, we examined how plot-level changes in tree abundance were associated with climate change and disturbance history. From the recent past (1983–2002, as a baseline) to the study period (2003–2022), MAT in the study region increased by an average of 0.7 °C (Extended Data Fig. 3). Drought frequency, determined based on the 12-month Standardized Precipitation–Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) in July (SPEI12July), generally increased, with the largest increases in southern provinces. Based on FIA records, recent disturbances recorded at T2 (less than or equal to 10 years before revisit) and legacy disturbances recorded at T1 (10–15 years before revisit) highlighted similar spatial patterns, but legacy disturbances affected smaller forest areas overall (Extended Data Fig. 4).

A generalized linear mixed model fitted across all species–ecosections revealed that climate, disturbance and their interactions were key drivers of stem abundance change (Fig. 2). Increases in temperature and drought frequency exerted modest but opposing influences on stem abundance: warming corresponded to gains, whereas greater drought frequency corresponded to losses. Baseline drought frequency partially mitigated the negative effects of increasing drought frequency on stem abundance, suggesting that forests historically exposed to more frequent droughts were more resistant to additional water stress.

Disturbances exerted strong effects on changes in stem abundance, and these effects differed between recent and legacy disturbances (Fig. 2). Recent fires were associated with the largest reductions in stem abundance, whereas legacy fires increased stem abundance, probably reflecting forest regeneration from earlier fires. Disease had generally weak effects, but legacy disease was associated with stronger negative effects than recent disease, suggesting more persistent impacts of earlier disease events. Conversely, recent insect outbreaks were associated with larger reductions in stem abundance than legacy outbreaks, consistent with partial recovery following earlier outbreaks. Moreover, where previous disease and insect outbreaks had occurred, recent fires were associated with greater declines in stem abundance (Extended Data Fig. 5), suggesting interactive and compounding disturbance impacts.

Fire effects also interacted with other factors including baseline drought, species’ fire tolerance and plant clade (angiosperm or gymnosperm) (Fig. 2). Specifically, fires in historically dry areas were associated with smaller reductions in stem abundance, probably because lower vegetation productivity and fuel availability in dry forests can limit fire severity and associated mortality33. Recent fire effects also depended on species’ functional traits, with fire-tolerant species experiencing smaller declines following recent fires. Legacy fire was associated positively with stem abundance in both plant clades, with substantially stronger responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms (Fig. 2a,b). Despite some variation, models in individual provinces were largely consistent with the overall effects (Extended Data Fig. 6).

In a recent development, to evaluate potential life-stage differences in responses to environmental change, we also modelled stem abundance change separately for saplings and adult trees (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5). Warming primarily promoted sapling abundance but had little influence on adult abundance. Although recent fires consistently caused declines in both saplings and adults, legacy fires showed a positive effect on sapling abundance but a negative effect on adults. This indicates regeneration events after legacy fires, but many recruits are still below the 12.7 cm DBH threshold at plot remeasurement (10–15 years after fire). Disease decreased adult stem abundance; recent disease had little effect on saplings and legacy disease was associated with reduced sapling abundance. Legacy fire effects on stem abundance differed between saplings and adults, and between angiosperms and gymnosperms. Legacy fire was associated with increased stem abundance in saplings, with substantially stronger responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. By contrast, legacy fire slightly reduced adult stem abundance, with no significant difference observed between angiosperms and gymnosperms (Fig. 2d,f).

Models of basal area dynamics showed patterns similar to adult stem abundance (Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8), reflecting a strong contribution of large trees to basal area. While MAT change had a marginally positive effect on basal area change (P = 0.056), drought frequency change and most disturbance factors showed negative effects, except for the non-significant effect of recent disease and positive effect of legacy fire. The positive effect of legacy fire was driven primarily by angiosperms, whereas gymnosperms showed relatively weak responses (Extended Data Fig. 7b,d).

To further understand the mechanisms underlying elevational shifts in tree abundance centres, we investigated how climate change and disturbance were distributed across species’ elevational gradients. We hypothesized that, rather than the average changes in environmental drivers across elevations, uneven exposure to the environmental changes between upper and lower range segments drives the observed elevational shifts in tree abundance centres. To test this hypothesis, we quantified differences in changes in climate (MAT and drought frequency) and disturbance extent between the two elevational segments (above and below the elevational centre at T1) for individual species–ecosections.

Overall, trees in upper-range segments experienced greater climate change and more extensive disturbance than in lower segments (Fig. 3). The upper–lower difference in the change in MAT (ΔMAT) was significantly positive for all the ecoregion provinces, indicating stronger warming at higher elevations (Fig. 3a). For drought frequency, lower range segments generally had higher values than upper segments during the baseline period (1983–2002), but this pattern partially reversed during the study period (2003–2022), with more ecoregion provinces showing higher drought frequency in upper segments (Supplementary Fig. 2). Consistent with this shift, temporal increases in drought frequency (ΔDrought) were greater in upper than lower species ranges in four ecoregion provinces, including Cascade Mixed Forest (M242), Sierran Steppe (M261), Arizona–Latest Mexico Mountains Steppe (M313) and Northern Rocky Mountain Forest (M333) (Fig. 3b).

Sources indicate that patterns of disturbance asymmetry varied by type and period (Fig. 3c–h). Notably, recent fire and disease exhibited significantly (P < 0.05) positive upper–lower differences in more provinces than their legacy counterparts. Specifically, recent fires affected larger proportions of forest area in the upper range in three of the seven ecoregion provinces, whereas the lower range was more affected in only one province (Fig. 3f). By contrast, there was no clear evidence showing the elevational asymmetry in legacy fire. Recent disease affected larger upper-range proportions in three provinces (Fig. 3g), compared with two provinces for legacy disease (Fig. 3d). Both legacy and recent insect outbreaks were more prevalent in upper-range segments in three provinces.

Recent findings suggest that we then modelled elevational shift rate in basal area and stem abundance, with species–ecosections as observational units and upper–lower asymmetries in climate change and disturbance as predictors (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 9). For basal area shifts, upper–lower difference in recent fire extent and insect outbreak extent showed significantly negative effects (P < 0.01), indicating that greater disturbance extents at one end of elevational range tended to displace population centres towards the opposite end. Elevational asymmetry in legacy fire showed a marginally significant positive effect on basal area shift on average (P = 0.053). The effect differed significantly between angiosperms and gymnosperms, with stronger upslope redistribution observed in angiosperms (Fig. 4a,b). Plant clade also showed a strong main effect, with angiosperms exhibiting more pronounced upslope shifts than gymnosperms under average covariate conditions across species–ecosections.

Sources indicate that for stem shifts, upper–lower difference in ΔDrought, recent fire extent and legacy insect extent demonstrated negative effects. Asymmetric warming (ΔMAT) showed a positive but non-significant association with elevational shift (P = 0.19), implying that warming may promote upslope movement weakly but is probably overshadowed by disturbance and increasing drought frequency. Interaction effects further revealed that species with higher fire tolerance were less sensitive to elevational asymmetry of recent fire extent, consistent with trait-mediated resilience to disturbance. Elevational asymmetry in legacy fire extent also showed a positive effect, suggesting that a greater legacy fire extent at one end of the elevational range was associated with a shift of the elevational centre towards the same end, potentially reflecting post-fire regeneration within previously burned areas. This positive effect was marginally stronger in angiosperms than in gymnosperms (Fig. 4c,d). Similar to basal area shifts, the main effect of plant clade indicated that angiosperms generally exhibited more pronounced upslope shifts than gymnosperms.

Industry observers note that across 212 species–ecosection combinations spanning broad climatic and biogeographical gradients in the western USA, many tree abundance centres remained relatively stable despite ongoing climate change and natural disturbance. This relative stability probably reflected opposing demographic processes, with ingrowth and growth promoted by warming and post-disturbance recovery counterbalanced by mortality associated with drought and disturbance. Where redistribution occurred, stem shifts were divergent, whereas basal area shifts were more commonly downslope (Fig. 1). Stem abundance is influenced more strongly by sapling ingrowth, whereas basal area is linked more closely to larger tree dynamics. The discrepancy between stem and basal area shifts suggests a general upslope redistribution of smaller trees relative to larger trees, consistent with previous findings that seedlings tend to occupy higher elevations than adults28. Elevational shifts in tree abundance centre arise from asymmetric changes in abundance along species’ elevational gradients (Extended Data Fig. 2) and therefore reflect demographic redistribution within species ranges in response to environment change.

In a recent development, our findings demonstrate that both climate change and natural disturbances, along with their interactions, are key drivers of tree abundance dynamics across the forests of the western USA. The strong negative effects of increasing drought frequency align with extensive evidence of drought-induced mortality and reduced growth under water stress34,35,36. In historically drought-prone areas, drought effects on stem abundance were weaker, consistent with evidence that previous or recurrent drought may enhance resistance to subsequent water stress through stress-memory mechanisms37. This pattern was more evident for sapling abundance than for adult stem abundance, suggesting that drought history may alter the balance between sapling mortality and sapling ingrowth more strongly. By contrast, warming exhibited positive effects on stem abundance, driven largely by enhanced sapling ingrowth or reduced sapling mortality (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5). This pattern suggests that temperature increases can promote regeneration where moisture remains sufficient38, which often occurs in cooler or higher-elevation sites.

Although fires, disease and insect outbreaks all reduce tree abundance, their effects unfold differently over time. Biotic disturbances such as disease and insect outbreaks caused prolonged declines, as pathogens and pests can persist for years and continue to kill trees39. By contrast, fires triggered abrupt losses in tree abundance followed by gradual increases during post-fire recovery and regeneration40. Our comparison of recent and legacy disturbances is limited to events recorded by the FIA annual inventory, which captures only a relatively recent disturbance history before plot remeasurement. Because post-disturbance recovery can unfold over longer time scales, earlier events not recorded in the FIA disturbance history may also have contributed to tree abundance redistribution but could not be evaluated directly in our analysis.

Sources indicate that post-fire regeneration has an notable role in changing stem abundance and elevational distributions, but its effects differed markedly between angiosperms and gymnosperms (Fig. 2). The relatively weak responses of gymnosperms to legacy fires are consistent with recent studies reporting widespread post-fire regeneration failure of gymnosperms in warm, dry and often low-elevation forests in the western USA41,42. When regeneration thresholds are crossed, fire can act as a tipping point: instead of returning to closed-canopy forest, sites may transition to shrubland, grassland or sparse woodland. By contrast, angiosperms highlighted relatively stronger positive responses to legacy fire, which aligns with the greater capacity for vegetative resprouting of many angiosperms following fires43. Such contrasting post-fire responses suggest that fires may increasingly promote divergent elevational redistribution between angiosperms and gymnosperms.

It has been revealed that although climate change and disturbance pressures drive tree abundance changes, their elevational asymmetry (differences between upper and lower range segments) emerged as an important predictor of the direction and magnitude of species’ elevational shifts (Fig. 4). Processes that reduce tree abundance including increasing drought frequency and recent disturbances can shift population centres away from the affected end of a species’ elevational range, whereas processes that enhance tree abundance such as warming and post-disturbance recovery at one end pull population centres towards the affected end. Under natural disturbance, stronger pressures in upper-range segments across the western USA (Fig. 3) were associated with more frequent downslope shifts in basal area. When plots affected by silvicultural treatments were included, however, basal area shifts were distributed more evenly between upslope and downslope directions (Supplementary Fig. 5), possibly reflecting the greater prevalence of timber harvest at lower elevations8. These results suggest that the elevational distributions can be modified by other elevationally asymmetric influences, including human activities. By explicitly quantifying these asymmetric environmental pressures rather than relying on area-averaged climate trends and disturbance, our approach captures the spatial heterogeneity that shapes demographic processes directly at species’ range segments. Although conceptually intuitive, such asymmetry has rarely been incorporated explicitly into broad-scale assessments of species redistribution. Our findings highlight the need to consider not only regional trends in climate and disturbance, but also how these pressures are distributed across elevation gradients.

Overall, natural disturbances and drought had stronger effects than warming in our models, probably reflecting differences in the time scales of demographic processes, including mortality, ingrowth and growth. Although natural disturbances and drought can reduce tree abundance rapidly through mortality, increases in stem abundance through ingrowth and in basal area through growth accumulate over time. Given the relatively short remeasurement interval (approximately 10 years) in this study, sapling ingrowth may be more evident than adult ingrowth, which may partly explain why adult stem abundance was less sensitive to warming and legacy disturbance than sapling abundance42. These differences in temporal sensitivity may also contribute to the different patterns of stem and basal area shifts. Basal area shifts, which are dominated by larger trees, were more commonly downslope and associated with greater disturbance activity in upper-range segments (Fig. 3). By contrast, stem shifts were more divergent, probably because sapling ingrowth can offset mortality losses more rapidly in smaller trees. Similar demographic differences may also underlie the contrasting redistribution patterns between plant clades. Angiosperms, which generally exhibit stronger recruitment and post-disturbance recovery43, revealed greater upslope redistribution than gymnosperms (Fig. 4b,d). This underscores the importance of long-term monitoring, as repeated measurements over longer intervals are essential for capturing the full demographic imprint of sustained warming and disturbance on species redistribution.

In a recent development, climate change may have exerted indirect effects on forest redistribution by altering disturbance regimes and their elevational distributions19,44,45. Although lower elevations in forests in the western USA were generally drier than higher elevations during the baseline period (1983–2002), drought frequency has increased disproportionately in upper-range segments in recent decades (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 2). This increase in drought frequency, together with stronger warming in species’ upper-range segments, may help explain the greater fire activity observed there23,24,46. Consistent with our findings, wildfires in the western USA have advanced upslope at an average rate of 7.6 m per year between 1984 and 2017 (ref. 24). Moreover, elevated winter temperatures have enabled mountain pine beetle (Dendroctonus ponderosae) to survive at higher elevations than previously possible, exposing previously less affected high-elevation forests to greater pest pressure47.

According to recent reports, our study underscores the substantial influence of disturbances, particularly wildfires and insect outbreaks, on tree abundance and elevational redistribution. Recent disturbances were often associated with reduced tree abundance, driving abundance centres shifting downslope. Meanwhile, climate warming and post-fire recovery tended to increase tree abundance, and post-fire recovery was associated with upslope shifts in tree abundance centres. Therefore, the combined pressures from climate change and disturbances place forest ecosystems in the western USA ‘between a rock and a hard place’. Given projected future climate change and increasing disturbance activities globally45, our findings highlight the need for continued monitoring and adaptive forest management strategies to mitigate these impacts and promote ecosystem sustainability and resilience.

Industry observers note that the annual inventory of the FIA programme uses a nationally consistent plot design (around 1 plot per 2,428 hectares (ha)) and provides remeasurements with consistent data collection procedures nationwide, enabling robust estimation of changes in forest structure and species distribution. Each FIA plot consists of four 168 m2 subplots on which adult trees (DBH ≥ 12.7 cm) are measured. Within each subplot, a 13.5 m2 microplot is nested to sample saplings (2.54 cm ≤ DBH < 12.7 cm)29. For some plots, additional macroplots are established to measure very large trees. To account for differences in sampling area among microplots, subplots and macroplots, we used the trees-per-acre expansion factors provided by FIA, which standardize tree abundance estimates to a common per-area basis. We obtained forest attributes from the initial inventory period (T1, 1999–2013) and the subsequent remeasurement period (T2, 2012–2025). Because forest management can influence regional patterns of tree density, we excluded plots that showed evidence of recent silvicultural activity, including harvesting, artificial regeneration or site preparation. A total of 44,368 forest plots located within montane ecoregions were selected across 11 western US states (Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, California, Utah, Nevada, Colorado, Arizona and Latest Mexico). The average interval between measurements was approximately 10 years.

In a recent development, elevational shifts were quantified within individual species–ecosection combinations, rather than across the entire western US, to avoid conflating elevational shifts with latitudinal shifts. Ecoregion boundaries followed the US Forest Service 2007 ecoregion map48. We selected 45 tree species that occurred in more than 100 remeasured FIA plots without evidence of silvicultural treatment within individual montane ecosections, yielding 212 species–ecosection combinations across 33 ecosections. For each species–ecosection, elevational shifts were quantified as the difference in the stem abundance-weighted or basal area-weighted elevational centres of all trees (DBH ≥ 2.54 cm) between the two inventory periods. The shift rate (metres per decade) was calculated by dividing the elevational shift distance by the mean remeasurement interval of plots where the target species was present. To examine spatial and taxonomic patterns, we further aggregated species–ecosection elevational shifts to the ecosection and species levels. For stem shifts, the mean shift for each aggregation was calculated using stem abundance as a weighting factor, whereas basal area was used as the weight for basal area shifts.

According to recent reports, because ecosection boundaries can intersect species’ elevational ranges, particularly at lower elevations, they may influence the observed elevational shifts by truncating portions of species distributions. To evaluate the potential impact of this boundary effect, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by extending montane ecosections into adjacent non-montane regions using spatial buffers. We applied buffer widths of 50 km and 100 km, which correspond roughly to the average width of counties in the western USA and are appropriate given the spatial uncertainty associated with FIA plot coordinate swapping within counties. Elevational shifts were recalculated under each buffering scenario and compared with the original estimates based on unbuffered ecosections. The overall distribution of elevational shifts remained highly consistent among the 0 km, 50 km and 100 km buffering scenarios (Supplementary Fig. 6). Therefore, we retained the original Bailey’s ecosections as the primary study units because buffering produced little change in the overall patterns.

This study aimed to examine how natural processes, including climate change and natural disturbances, influence tree elevational redistribution in montane forests in the western USA. Because silvicultural treatments often depend on local management objectives, ownership and socioeconomic conditions, we excluded plots that indicated evidence of recent silvicultural activity from the main analysis. As a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the elevational shift calculations with these plots included. This analysis produced more upslope shifts in basal area centres than the treatment-excluded analysis, resulting in a more balanced number of upslope and downslope shifts (Supplementary Fig. 5), possibly reflecting low-elevation timber harvest8. We therefore focused on the treatment-excluded analysis to minimize the influence of silvicultural treatments and better evaluate tree redistribution associated primarily with climate change and natural disturbances.

Sources indicate that to test whether the observed shifts in elevational centre were statistically significant, we used a non-parametric bootstrap resampling approach3,49,50. For each species–ecosection combination, FIA plots were treated as the resampling unit, and paired T1 and T2 observations were resampled together with replacement using the original sample size (Supplementary Table 1). In each iteration, elevational centres for both inventory periods and the resulting elevational shift were recalculated. This procedure was repeated 10,000 times to generate a bootstrap distribution of elevational shift estimates. From the distribution, we derived percentile-based 95% CIs and corresponding empirical two-tailed P values. A shift was considered significant when the 95% CI did not include zero. The two-tailed P value was calculated as twice the smaller proportion of bootstrap estimates greater or less than 0, representing the probability of observing a shift as extreme as the empirical value under the null hypothesis of no change.

In the FIA, plots are divided into conditions representing distinct landscape units based on attributes identified by field crews, such as ownership, land type (for example, forest, water) and evidence of disturbance. The proportional area of each condition within a plot is recorded. The FIA database records disturbance events on mapped forest conditions, such as fire, insect outbreak and disease, that occurred since the last measurement in a remeasurement or within the last 5 years for fresh plots. Only disturbance events affecting at least 1 acre (0.4 ha) in size (including both the plot and adjacent affected areas) and causing mortality or damage to at least 25% of trees were recorded51. Based on the recorded condition proportions, we calculated the total forest area and that disturbed by any of the three principal disturbance agents including fire, insect outbreak and disease in each plot at both the initial inventory (T1; legacy) and remeasured inventory (T2; recent). On average, legacy and recent fires occurred 13.1 and 4.1 years before the T2 remeasurement, respectively. Note that one plot could experience more than one type of disturbance agent, and the area was attributed to each agent based on its specific disturbance, resulting in possible overlap among disturbance agents. For each species–ecosection, we summed forest area and disturbed area from plots using FIA-defined expansion factors with the target species present and calculated the disturbance extent as the proportion of disturbed forest area to the total forest area at both inventories.

For climate variables, we used 800-m resolution monthly temperature data from the PRISM Climate Group Long-Term dataset52 (https://data.prism.oregonstate.edu/time_series/us/lt/800m/) and 4-km SPEI12July from the WestWide Drought Tracker53 (https://wrcc.app/climate/wwdt/archives). The PRISM long-term dataset was used because it is based only on long-term stations of record and is therefore considered more temporally stable than the PRISM All-Network dataset54. SPEI is a drought index calculated as difference between precipitation and potential evapotranspiration over a specified time period55. SPEI12July was used because it is correlated strongly with tree mortality and growth56,57,58,59,60. Drought events were determined as years with SPEI12July < −1.0 (refs. 57,58,61,62,63,64). MAT and drought frequency (number of drought years per decade) were calculated in the recent past (1983–2002) for a baseline and the study period (2003–2022). Climate change was calculated as the difference between these two periods, accounting for potential lags between climatic trends and vegetation responses1,65. For each species–ecosection, climate variables were extracted from all plots where the species occurred and averaged to obtain ecosection-level estimates.

Sources indicate that true FIA plot coordinates are not released publicly to ensure ecological integrity and protect landowner privacy. Instead, the publicly available FIA data apply a ‘fuzzing and swapping’ protocol. On public lands, plot locations are displaced randomly, typically by less than 0.8 km and rarely up to 1.6 km. For private lands, up to 20% of plots are swapped with another plot of similar attributes within the same county. Although these procedures introduce spatial uncertainty, their influence on our analyses is expected to be negligible for several reasons. First, plot elevation in the FIA data is generally accurate, and our analysis of elevational shifts relies on repeated measurements of the same plots, for which elevation remains constant across inventories. Second, around 76% of the plots used in this study occur on public lands with location offsets (<0.8 km). Although these offsets may introduce climate uncertainty because elevation and vegetation types can vary substantially within a single 0.8- or 4-km pixel, such mismatches are expected to be largely random across the large number of FIA plots (44,368) and therefore have limited influence on the overall conclusions of this study. Finally, for private plots, the swapping process pairs plots with similar forest type, stand size, latitude and longitude, ensuring that local climatic and ecological conditions remain comparable.

Sources indicate that we computed elevational asymmetry for relative tree abundance change (Extended Data Fig. 2), climate change and disturbance extent (Fig. 3) by calculating their difference between upper and lower range segments. Relative tree abundance change between T1 and T2 was quantified for stem abundance and basal area as a symmetric percent change, which places increase and decreases on a common scale (the average of T1 and T2) and avoids the asymmetry of conventional percent change66. Upper and lower range segments are defined as the elevational range above and below the elevational centre weighted by stem abundance or basal area from the initial inventory (T1). We also conducted analysis using plots within the uppermost and lowermost 25% of elevations and found similar patterns (Supplementary Figs. 1, 3 and 4).

Species attributes of fire tolerance, drought tolerance and plant clade (angiosperm or gymnosperm) were obtained from the US Department of Agriculture PLANTS Database (https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/). In PLANTS, fire tolerance qualitatively describes a species’ ability to survive or recover from fire and is classified into four levels: None, Low, Medium and High. Similarly, drought tolerance, describing a species’ ability to survive or maintain function under low soil moisture, is categorized into three levels: Low, Medium and High. For the four species lacking trait entries in PLANTS (Juniperus deppeana, Quercus arizonica, Quercus wislizeni and Quercus grisea), tolerance classes were assigned on the basis of expert knowledge. Detailed information on species attributes is provided in Extended Data Table 1.

We used a non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test to evaluate whether the upper–lower differences in climate change and disturbance extent were significantly different from zero (Fig. 2). We modelled the plot-level change in stem abundance and basal area between inventories using the log response ratio (LRR):.

Recent findings suggest that where \({M}_{T1}\) and \({M}_{T2}\) denote the values of stem abundance or basal area measured at T1 and T2, respectively, and c is a small pseudocount (set to 0.5 in this study) to avoid division by zero. Models were fitted in R using the glmmTMB67 package (v.1.1.10) with a Gaussian error distribution and identity link. Fixed effects included baseline climate and climate changes for MAT and drought frequency derived from SPEI12July, disturbance extents by fire, disease and insects during T1 (legacy) and T2 (recent), and species attributes including fire tolerance, drought tolerance and plant clade (angiosperm or gymnosperm). We also included interactions between baseline climate and climate changes, between baseline drought frequency and recent disturbance extent, and between disturbance and species attributes. Fire and drought tolerance classes were converted to continuous variables to facilitate model fitting. Plant clade was included as a categorical predictor using sum-to-zero contrasts (angiosperm = 1, gymnosperm = −1). All predictors except plant clade are standardized to zero mean and unit standard deviation before modelling. Species and ecosection were included as random effects. Because the models included several interaction terms (for example, climate change versus baseline climate), we evaluated collinearity among predictors using variance inflation factor. All predictors variance inflation factors less than 5, indicating acceptable collinearity, and no variables were excluded from the final models. For interpretability, model coefficients and their 95% CIs were later back-transformed from the log response ratio as \(100\times [{e}^{\beta }-1]\) and expressed as percentage changes in tree abundance associated with a 1 s.d. increase in each continuous predictor. Models were fitted for all plots across species–ecosections, separately for each ecoregion province, and for saplings and adult trees. The full models are provided in Extended Data Figs. 5 and 8.

Elevational shifts in stem abundance and basal area of species–ecosections were also modelled using glmmTMB with Gaussian error distribution and identity link. Predictors included the upper–lower difference in climate change, disturbance extent and their interactions (Extended Data Fig. 9). Species identity was included as a random effect. We also evaluated ecoregion province as an additional random intercept, but its variance was negligible and it had little influence on model results. Therefore, only species identity was retained in the final models.

According to recent reports, a, Basal area shift. b, Stem shift. Symbol size denotes relative tree abundance, calculated as the proportion of basal area or stem abundance relative to the total. Color indicates direction and magnitude of shift rate. Statistical significance of elevational shifts was assessed using two-sided paired bootstrap tests with 10,000 resamples. Significance levels are indicated as ***P < 0.001, **P < 0.01, *P < 0.05, and ·P < 0.1. Species are shown in phylogenetic order.

Recent findings suggest that a, Conceptual framework illustrating how differences in tree abundance change between upper (U) and lower (L) range segments predict elevational shifts. Increases (+) or decreases (–) in tree abundance at each segment lead to upslope (green arrows) or downslope (brown arrows) movement. b, Relative change in stem abundance (top row) or basal area (bottom row) at upper and lower segments for species-ecosections with significant (\(P < 0.05\)) elevational shift. Results are shown across size classes (columns; all trees, saplings, and adults) and different weighting schemes (rows; stem abundance and basal area). Points represent species–ecoregion combinations, colored by shift direction (green for upslope and brown for downslope). Numbers and percentages indicate the proportion of combinations showing significant shifts in each quadrant. Upper and lower range segments are defined as the elevational range above and below the elevational center weighted by stem abundance or basal area from the initial inventory (T1).

a, Change in mean annual temperature (ΔMAT, °C). b, Change in drought frequency (ΔDrought, dec−1). Drought frequency is the number of years per decade with SPEI12July < −1.0. Climate change is the difference in climate between the baseline period (1983-2002) and the study period (2003-2022). Each polygon represents a montane ecosection. Each polygon represents a montane ecosection. Climate change values for each ecosection were calculated using all FIA plots containing any of the studied species. The number of plots used to compute the ecosection-level averages are provided in the Source Data.

Each polygon represents a montane ecosection. The left column (a, c, and e) reveals the proportion of FIA plots affected by fire (a), disease (c), and insect (e) disturbances recorded in the initial inventory (T1), which generally occurred 10–15 years before remeasurement. The right column (b, d, and f) shows the corresponding proportions recorded in the second inventory (T2), typically representing disturbances within the past 10 years. Color gradients indicate the proportion of forest area disturbed within each ecosection calculated using all FIA plots containing any of the studied species. The number of plots used to compute the ecosection-level averages are provided in the Source Data.

Industry observers note that generalized linear mixed model coefficients are presented as percent changes in stem abundance between inventories associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in each predictor for (a) all trees, (b) saplings, and (c) adult trees (n = 74,448 samples for each analysis). Points indicate model coefficient estimates and error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. ΔMAT and ΔDrought represent temporal changes in mean annual temperature and drought frequency, respectively; drought frequency is the number of years per decade with SPEI12-July < −1.0. Fire, disease, and insect variables indicate the proportion of forest area affected by each disturbance before T1 (legacy) or between T1 and T2 (recent). All predictors except plant clade are standardized to zero mean and unit standard deviation before modeling. Plant clade was included as a categorical predictor using sum-to-zero contrasts (angiosperm = 1, gymnosperm = −1). Positive coefficients indicate increases in stem abundance, whereas negative coefficients indicate declines. The marginal and conditional R2 values were 0.153 and 0.165 for the all-tree model, 0.041 and 0.045 for the sapling model, and 0.170 and 0.191 for adult-tree model, respectively. Statistical significance was assessed using two-sided Wald z-tests without adjustment for multiple comparisons. Significance levels are indicated as ***P < 0.001, **P < 0.01, *P < 0.05, and ·P < 0.1. Exact P values are provided in the Source Data.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This season’s Premier League title race may be locked in a paralysed state of uncertainty but Arsenal, the defending champions, are determined to keep it interesting.
  • While the painful delay on Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict threatens to drag deep into next year, Arsenal are remaining hot on their tails.
  • City’s lead at the top is back to three points but Arsenal’s win here was unlikely to have sent any shivers down the spines of Enzo Maresca and his players in this phoney mess of a season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This season’s Premier League title race may be locked in a paralysed state of uncertainty but Arsenal, the defending champions, are determined to keep it interesting.

While the painful delay on Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict threatens to drag deep into next year, Arsenal are remaining hot on their tails.

In the ordinary course of a Premier League season, you would say Manchester City have applied pressure on Arsenal by opening up a six-point lead before the champions play at Nottingham Forest this afternoon.

This is not a normal Premier League season though, and we await to discover if the top of the league table is simply a mirage.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

According to recent reports, morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 26 Nov 2026 22:49.

Arsenal, Aston Villa and Manchester United have received a major boost in their pursuit of Club Brugge left-back Joaquin Seys, after the defender said he believes he is ready to move to a top club.

The 21-year-old Belgium international has become one of Europe's most promising full-backs since coming through the Belgian champions’ academy.

Reports suggest all three Premier League clubs watched Seys closely and made enquiries during the summer transfer window.

United saw him as a long-term answer to their left-back concerns, while Villa considered him a possible replacement for Lucas Digne.

Arsenal, meanwhile, could draw on the relationship established through the signing of Christos Tzolis.

Despite previously insisting he was solely focused on Club Brugge, Seys has now suggested to Het Laatste Nieuws that a high-profile departure could materialise at the end of the season.

"I believe you can go straight from here to a top club," Seys said via Sport Witness. "After all, with Club Brugge, we've already proven in the Champions League that we're on par with teams often viewed as 'stepping-stone' clubs. So, yes. I feel ready for it.".

The defender added that any summer exit will depend entirely on the specific project on offer, stressing he would never leave Brugge simply for the sake of a transfer.

Addressing the summer interest from England, Seys reiterated that nothing became concrete enough to push for an exit and insisted he was perfectly content when Brugge opted to keep him.

The young wide defender has backed up his growing ambition on the pitch this term, registering four assists in 12 Belgian Pro League outings alongside a goal against Lens and two assists against PSV Eindhoven in the Champions League.

Club Brugge have swiftly emerged as a favoured target for England’s biggest clubs after impressing on the European stage.

Arsenal raided the Jan Breydel Stadium for winger Christos Tzolis over the summer and are now competing with Man United for prolific striker Nicolo Tresoldi.

Seys is contracted until June 2029, leaving the Belgian club in a strong position should a summer bidding war develop.

However, the eight-cap international's public declaration that he is ready to take the next step is set to alert Arsenal, Aston Villa and United as they prepare their recruitment plans for 2027.

It has been revealed that inter led 2-0, then 3-1, then 4-2 at the Newly introduced Balance Arena on Sunday night. They still left Bergamo with a single point. The 4-4 draw with Atalanta left Chivu’s side third, three points behind leaders Lazio on 32 and now overtaken by Roma on 30.

Sources indicate that esposito gave Inter a two-goal cushion with his first two goals of the night. Elmas pulled one back for Atalanta on 35 minutes. Esposito restored the margin seven minutes after half-time to complete his hat-trick.

Four minutes later Zappacosta handled a Thuram shot on the goal line. Inter’s advantage was back to two goals once Sučić beat Sportiello with the resulting penalty.

De Ketelaere struck for a second time on 81 minutes. Bastoni’s handball then gave Atalanta a stoppage-time penalty, and Kessié converted it.

Chivu said his side had failed the exam in the final minutes. He called the result “two gifted points”. Esposito now has six goals this season, and no Inter player has scored more in Serie A.

It has been revealed that inter also lost Hakan Çalhanoğlu. He came off in the 33rd minute with a problem in the hamstring of his right thigh and is due to have tests on Tuesday 24 November, Sky Sport reported. He will miss Wednesday’s Champions League game against Stuttgart and Saturday’s league match with Genoa at San Siro. It is his second muscle injury of the season, after a layoff of about 20 days in September.

Juventus arrive at their own busy week in form. All four goals against Venezia came after half-time, from Woltemade, Koopmeiners, Cabal and a Kolo Muani penalty. The win came in Luciano Spalletti’s 600th Serie A game as a coach.

The direct test against Inter is further away. The league meeting between the two clubs is set for Sunday 10 January 2027 at 20:45.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 26 Nov 2026 23:15, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 23:57.

Brentford head coach Keith Andrews has revealed Josh Dasilva and Antoni Milambo could return to first-team action before Christmas.

Dasilva has been out of action since sustaining a hamstring injury while playing for Brentford’s B team in a Premier League Cup game against Wycombe Wanderers Under-21s in August.

Milambo, meanwhile, has not played first-team football since sustaining an anterior cruciate ligament injury while representing the Netherlands Under-21s in October 2025.

Dasilva and Milambo stepped up their recoveries with valuable minutes in Brentford B’s 2-1 win over Hull City on Sunday, with the latter scoring the opening goal at Wheatsheaf Park.

While the pair remain unavailable for Saturday’s Premier League clash against Manchester United, Andrews was able to offer a positive enhancement when asked whether the duo could return before Christmas.

“Yeah, that would certainly be the plan,” Andrews told reporters in Thursday’s pre-match press conference.

“We have a few games before then. They played 45 minutes the other night in the B team game. They both played well and came through the game well.

Industry observers note that “They’re building the fitness level that’s needed to come into the first-team space, but they’re training with us pretty consistently. They’ve been in and out to be ready for the B team game.

“They’ll continue that over the next week or two and then hopefully they can gatecrash the first-team squad.”.

In regard to other absentees, Brentford are unable to call upon the injured quartet of Nathan Collins, Aaron Hickey, Rico Henry and Kaye Furo.

Meanwhile, striker Igor Thiago will serve the second game of a three-match ban after being sent off in the defeat to Brighton & Hove Albion earlier this month.

Those available will be looking to build on Brentford’s impressive 4-0 win over Everton at the Gtech Community Stadium on Monday, which lifted the club up to sixth spot in the Premier League table.

#209295. What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1070 w)

Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one matter ranked above all others: the economy.
  • So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?
  • Sources indicate that markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one matter ranked above all others: the economy.

So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?

Sources indicate that markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory.

With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already noted he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, stated in a note.

"I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind.".

Sources indicate that some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.

Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, said the vote highlighted the extent of that opposition. Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.

"This election indicates that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he said. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted.".

It has been revealed that if the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown remarked, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.

According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center, 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.

That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.

Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.

According to recent reports, "Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office.".

Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.

According to recent reports, trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.

Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard said, the scale of the Republicans' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.

Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.

Were a deal to be struck with Iran, soaring energy prices — a pivotal election issue — could finally fall, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.

Industry observers note that "You've got to get a deal with Iran, and you've got to bring down gas prices," Kirkegaard said. "From a political point of view, that's the most vital thing now.".

It has been revealed that george Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he stated in a note.

Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.

Industry observers note that yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another issue vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.

That raises the prospect of the newly introduced Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic challenges to secure his political survival.

"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," Kirkegaard mentioned. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs.".

Despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle in trying to reverse them.
